Mr. Speaker, on a question of
privilege affecting myself and other members of the house, I should like to point out that in sessional paper No. 107-D, dated May 17, 1951, which was tabled yesterday, I find the following question by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) with the following answer by the government. This is the third question in that sessional paper, and it has reference to the site of the printing bureau in Hull. The question and answer follow:
Q. How much was paid for the site on which the building is being erected?
A. Estimated cost-$496,817.56.
On checking back I find that in sessional paper No. 107-B, dated March 27, 1950, the following question was asked by the hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Hodgson), and the following answer was given by the government:
Q. What was the cost of the site of the proposed printing bureau in Hull, Quebec?
A. Cost of the site to date, $824,979.72.
It is quite evident that an explanation is due from the minister as to this discrepancy, in that the answer tabled yesterday indicates a figure more than $300,000 less than the figure given on March 27 last year as to the cost to date.

subtopic: PRINTING BUREAU-REFERENCE TO INFORMATION GIVEN IN SESSIONAL PAPERS

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I regret very much to have to take a Toronto newspaper to task. I have always been taught that if a man hits you on one cheek you should turn the other, but when a newspaper hits you below the belt I think you have a right to stand up and fight. This paper accuses me of using my franking privilege to send out a pamphlet entitled, "Know Your Enemy." I absolutely deny that. Somebody must be using my frank in some illegitimate way, and therefore I say that that is hitting below the belt. They tell me that this pamphlet is anti-Semitic. If the Tribune condemns this pamphlet, then there must be some good in it. The pamphlet was just placed on my table; I looked at it only in a cursory way, but what I saw was good. It may be that I can find another issue of this pamphlet, because if it is as good as the first part then the world should know what the aim of this paper is.
I will not say any more on the matter. I will turn over the matter to the protective staff to find out who has been using my frank, and I will hand this paper to the Minister of Justice for future action.

subtopic: DEFINITION OF CANADIAN STANDARD YARD AND POUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Weights and Measures Act as passed in 1873 provided that a specified bronze bar would be the primary standard of length in Canada and a specified platinum-iridium weight would be the Canadian standard pound. With the progress of scientific metrology since 1873, it has been found that a more scientifically accurate primary standard can be defined in terms of the international metre. The bill now before the house for first reading therefore defines the primary standards of weight and measure in terms of the international metre and the international kilogram.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
During the discussion of this measure before the committee rose last evening, Mr. Chairman, a good deal was said about the income tax provisions in so far as they affect men and women in our active service forces overseas. A number of hon. members expressed the opinion that members of our active service forces overseas should be exempt from the provisions of the Income

Income Tax Act
Tax Act. In response to these suggestions it was explained that there were certain administrative difficulties; and it will be recalled that when this subject was brought up on an earlier occasion the Minister of National Defence pointed out the difference in dollars and cents that this exemption would result in as between a private in the ranks and a major general. Other considerations also have been put forward.
I suggest there are reasons why the recommendation that members of our armed forces on active service overseas should be exempt from the provisions of the Income Tax Act deserves further and favourable consideration by the Minister of Finance., It is not necessary to repeat the arguments that have been so well presented in favour of this exemption. However, it does seem necessary to refer to the fact that this was done during the last war. It is true there were administrative difficulties, as there would be today; but I submit that it is the duty of the government to decide what should be done and then take such steps as may be necessary to overcome any administrative difficulties.
This is something which particularly requires every effort on the part of the government, at a time when all Canadians are being asked to encourage enlistment in the armed forces. I submit the evidence is very strong that public opinion across Canada is overwhelmingly in favour of the suggestion that those who are offering life itself in the service of their country should be exempt from these taxes during their period of active service.
I recognize that hon. members should not regard as conclusive arguments the editorial point of view which may be expressed in newspapers across this country, important though that may be. But when there is a uniform request for this exemption, in very strong terms, on the editorial pages of the most responsible newspapers of Canada, we should recognize that it interprets public opinion without regard to political or other affiliations. Merely to look at some of the editorials which have taken a very strong stand on this matter one finds such words as "repugnant", "heartless", and terms of that kind used to describe the imposition of income tax on those on active service. I would refer to a statement such as this: "Imagine the public uproar if the defence minister ordered our soldiers in Korea to buy their own bullets". That statement, appearing in the Vancouver Sun, which is ordinarily very friendly to the government, merely indicates the sentiment being expressed from the Atlantic to the Pacific in regard to this tax.
Many anomalies can be suggested which indicate why such a tax would be most unfair. Let us consider, for instance, the case of a man killed in action-and unhappily we must recognize that we are called on to consider such cases; we are reminded of it from day to day by the casualty lists which indicate what Canada is suffering in a war, which is a very real war, being waged by the collective forces of the United Nations. Is the government going to make a claim against the estate of that man for arrears of income tax? Is the government going to pursue the ordinary course in regard to a debt of this kind? I am not raising this question for any other purpose than to illustrate one of the numerous difficulties that would arise and would have to be faced. I should think there would be a great reluctance to follow such a course. I am sure the Minister of Finance, a veteran himself, would be most reluctant to take such action. Then if that course is not right, the initial step should not be taken which would call for such action as an ultimate result.
I notice that a good deal of attention was paid to the fact that exemption from income tax would result in a substantial saving to a major general and a relatively small saving to other ranks. It may well be that there are discrepancies of the kind which require special consideration. I suggest, however, that that is no argument in itself. If it is right that the soldiers, sailors or airmen of the lowest non-commissioned rank should be exempt from this tax, the fact that someone else might be exempt in respect of a larger sum can surely be no conclusive argument against granting what would otherwise be regarded as a just allowance. As I recall the figure, it was estimated that for the lowest non-commissioned ranks the saving would be $6.85 per month. That, after all, does amount to some $80 in a year, which is not an insignificant figure in these days of rising costs of the necessities of life.
May I point out, Mr. Chairman, that on earlier occasions the government did not feel that this principle was so repugnant. It will be recalled that until comparatively recent times diplomatic and other representatives overseas in similar posts were exempted from income tax. As I understand it, that was done in recognition of the fact that those who served Canada outside of the country do not receive many of the conveniences, services, and amenities which are provided from the tax money which is paid. Furthermore, it was also a recognition of the fact that men and women who served Canada overseas are often called upon to bear dual expenses because of the necessity of maintaining a family or home in Canada, and also

other facilities of a similar kind overseas. Evidently the government decided that this was not a satisfactory method. The exemption was discontinued but in its place came the provision of generous living allowances and expense accounts, intended to recognize that in addition to the ordinary cost of carrying out services of that nature outside of Canada, there were also unusual expenses involved. Although the method is different, the government still recognizes that those who serve Canada outside of our national borders are faced with special expenses, quite apart from their daily living, that at least call for recognition. I submit that if it is appropriate that we should recognize our obligation to those who serve us in civilian capacities overseas, we certainly should recognize that same obligation to those who serve us overseas in uniform in a much more dangerous capacity.
Apart from the great danger, apart from the hardship and the separation from their families experienced by those on active service, which they willingly accept in offering their own services to their country, there nevertheless is the fact that those who go on active service outside of Canada in our armed forces do, for a considerable time, remove themselves from the opportunity to make use of the public services, the many public facilities and conveniences, which are available to the rest of us from the money paid in taxes to the government of Canada.
For that reason, in addition to the other reasons which have been so clearly stated, I believe that while men and women are on active service in our armed forces they should not be called upon to pay the full taxes required for all the services that they would ordinarily receive if they were in Canada. I believe the least that can be done for those who are making it possible for us to enjoy these services is to exempt them from those income taxes which bear particularly heavily on those who are receiving armed forces pay.
There are times when the government must follow a course which is not necessarily related to general public opinion if they believe that course to be more convenient and more satisfactory from the administrative point of view. I contend that in this case there are special reasons why the government should be very sensitive to public opinion as it has been expressed by the editorials in our	newspapers-which	often clearly
interpret public thinking-and by veterans organizations, municipal councils and other bodies which have taken a definite stand on this subject. We want everyone to feel that the utmost is being done to encourage young
Income Tax Act
men and women to accept the great responsibility they assume in becoming members of the armed forces of Canada. With the opinion that has been expressed so clearly by these various organizations, by veterans bodies and by the press as interpreters of public opinion, I urge that the Minister of Finance reconsider this particular request and indicate to the house that there will be an exemption from income tax for all members of our armed forces serving overseas.
East night there was some suggestion that this subject should be discussed in detail, and that hon. members of this house should say how this should be done or what alternative should be offered. I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that at this time we are considering a motion which says that it is expedient that certain things be done. As I understand it, the real purpose of the debate on this motion, and other similar motions, is that members of the house may indicate what they think is expedient or is not expedient. Then if their arguments have been sufficiently convincing, the minister responsible for the legislation which will be subsequently introduced has an opportunity to amend it accordingly before it comes into this chamber.
The point I am making, and the point I urge with the utmost earnestness upon the Minister of Finance, is that he should agree that it is not expedient to impose an income tax on those who are assuming the great responsibility of preserving freedom for Canada by taking their place in the armed forces of this country on active service overseas.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the leader of the opposition for the objective way in which he has dealt with this important question. I completely agree with the statement he made, and with the one that was made yesterday evening by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, to the effect that this is not a question which is to be determined on the basis of partisan politics or party interest. It is a question in which we are all interested, and our objective must be to do what is fair and just.
I again agree with my hon. friend that editorial comment does not necessarily indicate what public opinion is, although it is a fair indication of what a great many people feel. It was for that reason that I placed on Hansard yesterday evening a carefully-considered statement as to why I felt that an exemption from income tax for our armed forces was inequitable and unjust. I did not put it on the basis of administrative difficulties. At the end of my remarks, it is true, I referred to administrative difficulties, but

Income Tax Act
I expressly pointed out that this was not the important point, and that I was resting my case on the inequities and injustices created by such a system. As clearly as I could, I dealt with the history and with the reasons why I felt that it was unfair and unjust. I expressed the hope that those veterans who had had personal experience in the last war would give us the benefit of their views. 1 know that some have already done so. But I feel sure that the hon. member for Broadview could do so. He was of course a gallant officer; he had the benefit of these exemptions, and, by reason of the fact that he was an officer and fairly fortunately situated, would have received from that exemption substantial benefit, much greater benefit than the men serving under him. I myself never was in that position, but, speaking personally, I think I would feel uncomfortable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am being perfectly sincere. It is easy to get cheap applause for urging something of this kind; but I am trying to do what the leader of the opposition did, namely, deal with the matter objectively.
I stated that I thought that blanket exemption for those serving overseas would be unfair. To take the case of the private who is in Korea today, as my hon. friend pointed out, his income tax liability is $6.85 a month if he is single. In the case of officers, of course, it is much higher. As against that he receives a tax-free foreign allowance now of $9 a month, which is in excess of his income tax liability.
The purpose of the resolution which is now before us, or the legislation which will be based upon it, is to provide that, as to service pay and allowances, if a man has no other income his total tax liability will be discharged by a special total deduction and he will not be even obliged to file an income tax return. Therefore the case which my hon. friend mentioned, that of trying to collect income tax from a soldier who had been killed, could not arise under those circumstances. Any liability which might exist would have been discharged as he went along.
After the most careful consideration, I have come to the conclusion which I have indicated, namely that of a blanket exemption for those who are serving overseas creates the most manifest inequities and injustices. It is for that reason that I am strongly opposed to it. I think that recognition of the service offered by our soldiers should take some other form than that of a blanket income tax exemption.

I suppose that one should not always argue by analogy, but I think there must be some reason, which is probably similar to the one I am putting forward now, why a similar practice should have been followed in the British forces and in the American forces. I am aware of the fact that we did it in the last war. Last night I indicated the historic sequence of events, how from time to time we had to amend it, and the difficulties that we got into in doing it. Such a system might create incentive to keep people in the field rather than back at headquarters; but honestly, from the best consideration I have been able to give to it, that is the only justification I can see.
If we look at this thing objectively and dispassionately, and try to disabuse our minds of the admittedly strong emotional appeal of an exemption of this kind, I would hope that we would come to the conclusion that there should not be any over-all blanket exemption such as is suggested, but that such recognition as may be appropriate should take the form, as it does now in the case of other ranks in Korea, of a tax-free foreign allowance. I would hope that those who have had personal experience in the last war-and I did not have it, although I had a bit of experience by being in touch with it through my association with the Department of Finance during that period- would give me the benefit of their views as to how it worked out and whether they honestly, sincerely and conscientiously believe that it was a fair system.

That is what existed. I am
sorry if I misled by hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All service pay and allowances were exempt. I can give an example-I will not take anyone in the chamber. There is a friend of mine in Montreal who was in one of the high brackets. I think ninety-six per cent of his top dollar was taken in taxes. His rank

during the war was that of major. The exemption which he got through serving overseas meant that he got virtually his whole pay, whereas if he had not had that exemption, a substantial amount would have been taken in taxes. It is perfectly obvious that a man benefits who either has high service income or high outside income. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said that last night. I do not know whether my hon. friend read what I said.
Yes, I read it. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was a statement that I tried to make as comprehensive as I could. I set out the history in detail. We had fellows flying into an income tax free position and floating into an income tax free position. I would hate to be thrown back into that sort of situation again. I am sure that the committee will appreciate the fact that the revenue implications of this suggestion are relatively negligible.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The suggestion that I have been hinting at, that is, of some form of combat pay or foreign service pay, would probably be considerably more expensive from the point of view of the treasury. But I suggest that it would be infinitely fairer than this haphazard impact of a general exemption of service pay and allowances, either for overseas service or otherwise. It is for that reason that I urge that all members consider this matter carefully. I should like to suggest that we do not attempt to decide it on this resolution. In this resolution I am providing for the authorizing of a simplified form of income tax liability for all service personnel who are serving in Canada or abroad. But that does not preclude another provision to the effect that they shall be entirely exempt.
The consideration I have given to the matter up to the present time will not enable me to conclude that the fair and proper thing to do would be to revert to the practice which we followed in the last war. Now, perhaps views may be put forward which will persuade me that that is wrong. I am not under any illusions as to what the easy course to follow would be. The easy thing to do would be simply to follow the practice which prevailed in the last war. I am sure that hon. members will give me credit for believing that the view which I am putting forward
Income Tax Act
is not with the object of gaining any immediate popularity. While I may be mistaken, it is put forward because I believe it is in the best interests of the servicemen themselves and the taxpayers as a whole.

Certainly anyone would be impressed by the dispassionate way in which the leader of the opposition and the Minister of Finance have discussed this matter. However, as an example of the unfairness of granting a general blanket exemption the minister mentioned an officer who had a private income. My suggestion to him was that so far as service pay and allowances are concerned, they should be exempt. Certainly there is not much at stake from a monetary standpoint. If the entire force in Korea today were taxed the total amount would not exceed $1 million.
Some time ago the Minister of National Defence gave as his reason why the system that was followed during the last war could not be followed at this time, that a brigadier overseas, with a large income, would be exempt from income tax. That argument is not a very powerful one. The brigadier would pay approximately $120 a month in income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be $142.90.
I was just figuring it out roughly. It is $142.90 for one brigadier. How many colonels are there?
Four. The colonel's tax is $97.35.

Well, the number of officers over the rank of lieutenant would not be very large. The position there is that the many who receive the small rate of pay of $2.35 a day, the privates, and beyond that of course the non-commissioned officers, would have to pay tax in order to prevent the senior officers from escaping the payment of tax. Looking at the situation from the broadest standpoint, and aside from any sentimental consideration at all, the people of Canada as a whole ask that this exemption be given. Generally speaking, I think that members in all parts of the house-I know of no exceptions, although there may be some-are in support of the idea, as are the people generally.
I feel that even though the minister has rather categorically closed the door to consideration, the desires of the people of the country as a whole should be effectuated. There may be difficulties in administration.

No serious difficulties; I took it from what the Minister of National Defence said the other day that there were, and the only reason is that it might create inequities. If that is so, then I feel that that of itself is not sufficient, because after all, the only reason for objection to inequities is that they are felt by others. I know of no person in this country who would feel it was inequitable to allow those who serve to be exempt from income tax on their pay and allowances

and I refer to those who serve today in Korea.
Members of parliament have an exemption of $2,000 a year. I know there are some who regard that as inequitable, but I know of no one who would say that an exemption to the men who serve in Korea would be inequitable. Let me give you an example. In the Department of External Affairs we have on foreign service many competent officials. They pay income tax on their income, but they do not pay on their allowances. The result has been that in recent years, while the pay has not gone up, the allowances have mounted. I ask any hon. member to look at the record of public accounts for 1950 at page E-20. These allowances are substantial. While I do not suggest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the allowances have increased as a form of indirect exemption, the fact remains that they have materially increased in recent years.
I am just reading indiscriminately from these allowances. I am not speaking of the salaries of $16,000 a year and so on. Allowances, $13,092,	$15,366,	$15,000,	$12,192,
$23,592, $13,836, $13,992, $16,092. I pick out the larger ones as well as the smaller ones- $10,092, $12,792, $25,320, $12,552, $14,892, $13,536. The last one on the list is Pakistan, and it is the last one I gave. No one has suggested that these allowances are inequitable. In addition to these allowances the recipients receive removal expenses, travelling expenses and the like. These allowances are given in part because the officer on foreign service, as the leader of the opposition said, does not enjoy the benefits that his taxation would grant to him were he within this country.
I do not want to engage in any sentimental discussion. I went to the reading room about

a week ago and I read the editorial comment across the country, in publications of different political persuasions, and without exception the general demand that was voiced was for the granting of this exemption. For instance, here is what the Windsor Star said in an editorial on May 14:
Making it worse.
The federal government's arguments against income tax exemptions for service men on overseas duty are going from bad to worse.
The latest, offered by Defence Minister Brooke Claxton, is that it's difficult to devise a system of exemptions that would be fair to all concerned. By way of example he said that if the forces overseas were relieved of all income tax liability, a major general would gain $172.30 a month and a first-class private only $6.85.
But a major general is at the divisional command level, and for every officer of that rank there are about 10,000 privates. Does this mean that to keep one major general from saving $172.30 a month in tax, the department is willing to nick the privates for $68,500?
As it happens, we haven't a major general in Korea, nor are we likely to have one there or in Europe for some time. Our highest officer in Korea is a brigadier. Are 6,000 or 7,000 privates to be clipped for $6.85 a month each, therefore, just to keep one brigadier from saving about $120?
Our financial wizards in Ottawa should come down to earth.
That represents the general viewpoint today. The minister has stated that it is not a question of administrative difficulty; it is the inequities or anomalous conditions that would be created. There would be no anomalous condition or inequity created if the pay and allowances were exempted. A person with a private income would make out his income tax return the way we do, and on top of page 2, I think it is, he would show as an exemption his pay and allowances from the armed forces the same way as we show our $2,000 allowance.
The inequity is caused by a few people having the idea that they are being discriminated aganst, that something unfair is being done. I cannot think of anyone in this country who would consider that an inequity was being created by exempting the pay and allowances of those who are serving in the armed forces. I hope the minister will have his officials look into this matter. It is little things like this that, while unimportant-the minister says it is only a matter of $1 million of revenue-undermine morale. It is this kind of thing that causes a feeling of resentment. It is this kind of thing that, as we all know, whether we sit to the right or the left of the Speaker, creates those pinpricks, those difficulties that so often undermine spirit and morale.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As the hon. member suggests, I shall give consideration to all the views that are voiced today. But in order to keep

the record straight I should like to point out that under the Income Tax Act the allowances of our diplomatic officials who are serving abroad are subject to exemption, and the same exemption applies to members of the military or air forces of Canada who are serving abroad and who are receiving allowances.

Mr. Chairman, we in this group strongly support the suggestion that the pay and allowances of men in the armed services fighting overseas should be exempt from income tax. To my mind there is something revolting about the idea that a man who is fighting for his country and who may be called upon any day to make the supreme sacrifice should also be required to contribute toward the financial cost of the war. Surely his sacrifices should be regarded as full payment on his part toward the cost of the war without his being required to make any other financial contribution.
We must remember that these men when they come back, if they are lucky enough to come back, will be required, by means of taxation in the years to follow, to contribute toward the cost of the war they have fought. Yesterday the minister mentioned the fact that there is no income tax exemption in Great Britain and the United States for men of the armed services. Surely the minister would not say that he supports everything that is done by the governments of Great Britain and the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know of any country where complete exemptions are allowed.

The minister must be aware of the fact that in Great Britain and the United States there is compulsory military service. Canada and Iceland are the only two countries that have not compulsory military service. There is a big difference between a country that has compulsory military service and a country that has a voluntary system.
If we had in this country a compulsory system whereby every man would have to go into the armed services at the age of eighteen years, we would be spreading the burden equitably across the whole country. But where you have a voluntary system there is no equality of service and sacrifice. In some cases whole families are wiped out. I know a case in the last war where five or six sons in a family were wiped out. That is not equality of sacrifice. I do not think the minister is making a fair comparison when he compares Canada, where there is voluntary service, with countries having compulsory service.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We had compulsory service in the last war.

The minister is aware of the fact that it is highly desirable that during his term of service a soldier should save as much money as possible toward the day when he must re-establish himself. The minister knows that the benefits granted by the veterans legislation are not sufficient to reestablish these men. The minister knows also that, judging from what has happened in the past, the veteran is usually discharged in a period of inflation during which he must face the added difficulty of re-establishing himself when prices are high.
While we have the dependents allowance board, many soldiers serving overseas are having to make substantial contributions toward the upkeep of their family made necessary by the high cost of living. Yesterday the minister gave a number of reasons why he thought exemption should not be granted to the members of the armed services.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. member advocating a general exemption for members of the armed services, or only for those serving in some foreign theatre?

For those serving overseas. The minister referred to senior officers and stated that the benefits they would receive would be so much greater than those received by the men in the ranks. The minister has dealt with that point himself and shown how that difficulty was overcome in the last war. As reported on page 3152 of Hansard of May 17, he said:
Any single member of the armed forces with an income of less than $1,600 was exempt, and married members were exempt at higher amounts. In addition a complicated tax credit formula was employed to gradually increase the tax above those exemptions until the full rate of tax was paid.
We could give the men in the ranks an exemption of $2,000 in the case of single men and $3,000 in the case of married men, and then steeply graduate the income tax above that so that the officers in the higher ranks would be paying the full amount of the tax.
The minister referred also to the difficulty of deciding who would benefit. That is a problem that is faced by the Department of Veterans Affairs in all their legislation. In every act it has been necessary to define just what type of veteran will benefit. For instance, under the War Veterans Allowance Act the beneficiary is the man who saw service in a theatre of real warfare. Under the Veterans Land Act the beneficiary is the man who saw service overseas or who served twelve months in Canada. I presume that if exemptions are granted from income tax the eligibility will have to be defined carefully,

Income Tax Act
but it should not present any greater problem for the minister than has been presented in the veterans legislation.
I should like to say once again that we must realize that the men who are fighting our battles today are paying their full share of the war; therefore it would not be fair to ask them to pay income tax, because in doing so they would be bearing a double share.

On behalf of this group I should like to express our support for the idea that the men serving in Korea should be exempt from income tax. I am pleased that the discussion has been kept on a nonpolitical basis, and that we are discussing the question in a straightforward manner in an effort to find a solution. I am sure that the minister is as anxious as we are on this side of the house to do the best possible. I do not think the administrative difficulty is such that it cannot be overcome.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not insurmountable. I have said time and time again there is no insurmountable administrative difficulty.

Then the only basis on which you can argue that you should continue the tax is that inequities might arise if the tax were not left in effect. I think that can be overcome. It is true that there were many difficulties during the last war when our troops were serving in a great many theatres. There were many different types of cases that had to be dealt with, but at the present time that is not so. We are only fighting in one theatre of war, and it seems to me that the difficulty experienced in the last war would be much less today. If the minister thinks there would be inequities between senior officers and privates at the present time, may I point out that there are very few senior officers involved, and therefore that is not an argument at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend appreciates what I said, that it is not only the inequity between officer and private but between one soldier and another.

If that is the obstacle, then I think the way to avoid it is to give an exemption of $1,000 on the pay of men in combat service overseas. You do that for men over sixty-five years of age. You give them an additional $500 exemption. If an additional exemption of $1,000 were given on the pay and allowances of men in combat service then that would take care of practically all ranks below that of captain. From every point of view that one can look at the matter it seems to me that something should be done at this time. I have read the newspapers, and I have not seen one organization expressing an opinion on this matter that has not
[Mr. Quelch.l
asked the government to give consideration to exempting these men. The minister admits that there are no administrative difficulties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say there were none. I said there were no insurmountable difficulties.

No insurmountable difficulties. There have been difficulties in the application of all income taxes ever since 1940 when we started to raise income tax levels. We have had to make amendments to the act to do away with inequities and to make it fairer. Therefore it does not seem to me that is a sound argument at this time. I urge the minister to give serious consideration to granting an exemption of at least $1,000 on the pay of men serving in active combat service for this country at the present time. As the hon member for Lake Centre indicated, it is the little pinpricks that very often carry more weight than something much more important. If it is possible to avoid them I think we should.

Having brought this matter to the attention of the government on at least three other occasions, I feel compelled to again voice my support at this time because I believe the minister is perhaps softening up somewhat and will make the necessary change to meet the wishes of members of the house.
Paragraph 4 of the resolution reads:
That the governor in council be authorized to make regulations under which the income tax of members of the armed forces on their service income will be paid in full in respect of the pay and allowances of each pay period by a deduction therefrom in accordance with a special table subject to the right of any member to file a return on an annual basis.
Right from the start I have resented the principle of taxing men who are fighting overseas. A reading of this particular section makes me feel all the more resentful of the implications contained therein. The hon. member for Acadia has put the position very well. I feel that by giving single men an exemption of $2,000 and married men an exemption of $3,000 we would get away from quite a few of the inequities involved in this proposition. Last night the Minister of Finance suggested giving additional foreign service pay. In my opinion that is another way of passing the buck to the Minister of National Defence, and if this legislation is passed he will again throw it back to the Minister of Finance. By doing what has been suggested by the hon. member for Acadia, the pay and allowances of those in the higher pay brackets would be adequately taken care of. I think there is something the matter with the principle of this legislation and I should like to see it corrected before it is passed.

I had not anticipated participating in this debate, but I feel that the minister has given a very dear-cut statement with respect to the inequalities that would arise from the adoption of the program now being supported by the opposition. I should like to go back to the years of the first world war. As the hon. member for Lake Centre has stated, the pay is now more than 100 per cent greater than what it was from 1914 to 1918.
So is the income tax.

It is very difficult for any member of the house to prevent himself from rising to speak on a question which by and large may be viewed at the moment as a popular one to support. It has been stated -and I recognize the truthfulness thereof

 that there has been more or less of an uproar in the editorials of various newspapers across Canada with respect to this particular tax. If we look back I think we will find many instances in the past where for the moment a particular topic was popular with a great number of people, and to get up and kick about it was the popular thing to do. It is very hard for a person to resist doing that at this time. However, I think that we should look at this matter objectively, as the minister has stated. I have talked, as other hon. members have, with a great number of men serving not only in Canada but also in Korea. It has been stated during the debate that at the present time we have no major generals serving in Korea. That is quite true, but we unquestionably have a large and ever-increasing number of higher officers in the service. I do 'not think for a moment those to whom I have spoken would strenuously object to the payment of income tax. When we went overseas in the first world war there was no question of income tax, of course, because it was not in existence then; but neither was there in the minds of any of those who went overseas at that time any question of social security while they were serving or when they returned.
These are matters we should keep in mind. I believe the government made a mistake when they exempted $2,000 of a member's indemnity from the payment of income tax. I believe that, otherwise I would not be on my feet now. As lawmakers for Canada I think we should be taxed on our entire indemnity. Whether or not that indemnity is too low is another question, but I do not believe we should have an exemption, because we set a very poor example to the electorate throughout Canada. There are plenty of people in this country today on fixed incomes who will be in a very poor position to pay the income tax they will be 80709-202
Income Tax Act
charged. It is true that they may not go on active service either now or in the years to come, though there are thousands of such people who are preparing for active service or going on service today, to whom the income tax does not mean tuppence. I believe, and I would be prepared to maintain my stand before the various returned organizations of this country, that these people do not wish any particular preference. They want to serve their country in the way they can serve it best. Fundamentally it is a question of service to the country on the part of those men now in the active services, and the women who will be enlisted under plans which have been announced. They are desirous of giving something to the country, not of getting something from the country. So I sincerely and honestly believe there is not nor will there be any great resentment in the armed services of this country as a result of the imposition of income tax.
The Minister of Finance has stated that there would be no insurmountable difficulties with respect to the administration and collection of that tax. I do not wish to disagree with him, but I think because of his kindliness he may have minimized those potential difficulties as much as possible. We have an increasing number of men serving in various parts of Canada, and who will be serving in Europe and in Korea. We have stepped up our program with respect to technical personnel. We know that plans being followed today may be completely outmoded two or three months from now. As a result we may have large numbers of men being transferred from Korea to Canada or from Canada to the United Kingdom or from the United Kingdom back to Canada. I believe the difficulties that would arise because of that constant shifting of personnel would be very great.
As far as pay is concerned, as I have said the ordinary man in the ranks will never become a millionaire; but the fact remains that he is getting over 100 per cent more than we got in the first world war. I really believe the great majority of those in our armed services today will not resent the imposition of income tax at all. Rather I believe they will welcome it, because they want to see our whole defence program speeded up and they know the money taken from them in that way will increase rather than lessen the ability of this country to give them the necessary equipment in the shortest time possible, so that in the words of Winston Spencer Churchill they may be able to go on and finish the job. I do believe that with respect to this question of income tax we should completely divorce our thoughts from an appeal which may be

Income Tax Act
*popular for the moment. I am sure those in the armed services are not anxious that their stay in foreign lands should be prolonged, and the contributions they make in this way, small though they may be, will give them confidence that they will be able to conduct the war against the present enemy, and against any future enemy, to a successful conclusion so they may return to their homes and loved ones as soon as possible.
The hon. member for Lake Centre quoted a number of figures showing the allowances made to those in the foreign service. I am rather inclined to believe that those allowances may be out of proportion, though I do not know; I have not gone into the question. It seems to me, however, that the soundest way to look at this proposition is to realize that whatever our contribution may be by way of taxes, that money is going to assure victory and peace; to think of what we as Canadians are going to have after the money has been spent, and what would be our situation if the money to carry forward our preparedness program was not forthcoming. The alternative could quite easily be defeat. I cannot help but think of the words of the president of France who honoured us with a visit not long ago, and who said it was not so much a matter of the cost as long as the result was peace. I believe those words would be repeated by thousands of our fighting men, no matter where they are. The things they want are the tools of war. They want the war prosecuted with thoroughness and effectiveness. They want to have the most modern arms and equipment. It is our duty as legislators of the Dominion of Canada, Mr. Chairman, to keep our eye constantly fixed on the goal, and to see that these men are given just that. We can best do it by the quickest consummation of our whole program with respect to taxation, and our program to prevent aggression, in order that victory may result and peace be assured.

Mr. Chairman, while listening to the last speaker I felt sorry that he had not paid some attention to the tone set by the Minister of Finance in this debate. The minister correctly said that this is not a political issue. This is a matter in which all members of this house are equally concerned, and for which they are trying to find a solution in the best interests of the men about whom we are speaking. The hon. member for Vancouver -Burrard certainly got away from that. His case was very weak. He took the advice I have heard given by some of the ministers of the church here: when your case is weak holler very loud. He did not have much of a case, and I am sure everyone could hear him.
{Mr. MacDougall.]
This is not a popular issue, but is an honest endeavour by everyone who has spoken to find the best solution. I do not think the hon. member contributed very much towards the solution.
I listened to the minister's statement, and then I read it over very carefully. I agree with most of what he said He definitely came to the committee and said: this is a problem; I do not think I have the solution. He posed the problem for us. Solutions have been offered, and I think some of them are workable. I agree with the minister that a blanket exemption is not the thing. I believe that the method, which would cause the least. administrative difficulty, and which would relieve the people we are thinking about, is to grant another $1,000 exemption. The hon. member said that the $6.85 received by a private who is sleeping in a foxhole in Korea would buy a lot of equipment for him, but that does not mean very much to the private.
Will the hon. member repeat that? I did not hear it.

To the private soldier this $6.85 is a lot of money. It represents a lot of beer.
I know it means a lot to the private, because I have gone through the experience. When you go into a canteen without that $6.85 it is not so nice. That is the fellow I am concerned about, the fellow getting the $6.85 monthly tax. I should like the minister to consider granting another $1,000 exemption which would take most of these people we are worrying about out of the tax brackets altogether. Everyone concerned would get relief to the extent of the extra $1,000 exemption. The brigadier and the lower ranking officers would' get that bit of relief, and they would be grateful for it. The department would not lose very much in taxes from the top group, but it would completely relieve those in the lower brackets; that is the $6.85 tax a month chaps, the men who do most of the fighting. The other fellow just directs it. I believe this extra $1,000 exemption would get us over the difficulty.
I do not believe -combat pay is the answer.
I think that is an excuse which has been set up. This combat pay arrangement creates more administrative difficulties. You have to have an extra staff to decide who is a combat soldier and who is not, who should receive the exemption. Then, the department takes it back in taxes. There is no doubt in my mind that the tax department will find a way of getting back that combat pay. I am not saying the minister will do that, but there are people behind him who are rather adept at getting back as much as possible. I do not feel combat pay is the

answer. I believe it creates a lot of administrative headaches. Now we know who are in Korea, and we have them on the tax rolls. We could do as we have already done on two occasions. I want the member for Vancouver-Burrard to note this carefully. A tax exemption was granted to corporations under $10,000 ip that the surcharge did not apply, and then there was a special exemption of $500 for men over sixty-five years of age. This exemption business is not new. It would foe a simple matter to write in that additional exemption of $1,000, and in my opinion it will take care of the problem.
The hon. member made another point that is not germane to this discussion at all. I do not know why he dragged it in, but he mentioned the $2,000 exemption granted to members. Anyone in this house who feels that he cannot use that or who feels he is doing anyone an injustice by getting it, can return it or can declare it as taxable income. He can pay taxes on it. Sometime someone is going to raise that question in this house and give it a real analysis. I consider that the members of parliament who sat here all during the war-many of them lost a lot of money-were the greatest suckers in Canada. They fought for everybody in the country. Everyone got tax relief for the amount of money he spent in earning his income, that is everyone except members of parliament. A lot of members went into debt to the extent of $2,000 or $3,000 a year in order to stay here. I have never felt a bit reluctant about taking it. I considered I was entitled to it. Sometime this question has to be opened up, but I have not any intention of doing so now. I would suggest that any hon, member of this house who feels as the member for Vancouver-Burrard indicated, that it is a wrong thing to do, should return the money or pay taxes on it.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I did not say anything of the kind. The hon. member is misinterpreting what I said. I did say this, and I maintain it, that as legislators of the Dominion of Canada we should not be the ones to place exemptions on our own salaries. I did not say that we are not entitled to it. I believe we are entitled to that and more. .
I am not going to argue with the hon. member, but I am glad he came around to my way of thinking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are going to forget the soldiers pretty soon.

I should like to leave the idea of that $1,000 exemption with the minister. Will the minister say whether the soldier in the field receives a living allowance-I think 80709-202J

it amounted to $1.37 in the last war and was called a field allowance-and is that allowance included in his income for tax purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know about field allowances. I am told that a married man receives what is known as a separation allowance if he is serving away from home. That is tax exempt. I think what the hon. member for Cape Breton South had in mind was as to what was reckoned as the equivalent of meals and quarters which serving personnel would receive-I think that was calculated at something like $1.37 a day-or whether, as to those who pay tax in Canada on pay and allowances, their income from the services was reckoned including that amount which they were calculated to receive for meals and quarters, and that their total income was assessed on that basis. The question asked by the hon. member for Cape Breton South is whether the income of those who pay income tax today is calculated by including the value of their meals and quarters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I am not too familiar with the present-day scale of pay and allowances; but I am informed that for the purpose of computing income tax, pay and allowances consist of basic pay of rank for officers, plus two-thirds of the allowances for rations and quarters. Then there is separation allowance when they are serving away from their families which is tax-exempt. But I will inform myself a little more fully as to the allowances.

I should like to express to the minister for what it is worth my own personal comment. I think that the hon. member for Cape Breton South, when he was speaking, stated the problem well, and I must congratulate him on the way he did it. I am glad to see the attitude taken by the minister, by the leader of the opposition as well as by all those who have spoken in this debate. They have kept the discussion on a high, non-political plane. I would certainly hope that the minister would give the matter his consideration, and I know he will. I .should like to see this $1,000 exemption taken into consideration.
Should the item not stand,. Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. Perhaps I might say at this point that I am glad to have had this discussion, and I am glad to have the views of all hon. members on this question. As I said at the beginning-and as others have said-I feel strongly, as I know we all do, that this matter should not be treated on the basis of party politics at all. I hope it will be settled on the basis of what is right and fair and not on the basis of emotion or sentiment. That is what I have been striving for, and I am sure that is what all bon. members have been striving for. I am sorry that so far most if not all *of those who have spoken have been my fellow veterans of the first world war when we did not have any income tax problems. In considering the matter, I think we should project our minds a bit farther forward than Korea, as indicated by the hon. member for Melfort, because it is anticipated that we shall have troops serving in Europe as part of the integrated force; and I think we should give consideration to what may be the situation there.
As I have tried to indicate, this is far from being a simple problem. I too was impressed and interested in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South; and I am quite prepared to study that suggestion and all suggestions that have been made. I want to emphasize again the fact that this is not a matter of fundamental government policy. We want to do what is the right thing here, and what the members of the House of Commons, representing the Canadian people, want. But I want to be sure that there is full and adequate discussion of all sides of the thing so that, so far as possible, we do the right thing. I do not believe that what we did in the last. war was the right thing; and that is the only reason that I have been attempting to put forward the suggestions which I have been putting forward.
If this meets with the approval of the *committee, I would hope that we would pass this resolution as it stands. We have to bring in a bill. I shall be glad if any others who have views to express will voice them. We have not as large an attendance here this afternoon as we sometimes have. There may be others whose views on this question would be valuable. I should like to get the bill distributed and made available to members. But I am quite prepared to give an undertaking that if we come to the conclusion that some change is desirable, it can be made of course when we have under consideration the section of the bill relating to service pay. I think that is the practical way to deal with the matter.
I am quite sincere when I say that I am anxious to get just as many points of view
[Mr. Coldwell.l
on this thing as possible. It may be that a suggestion of some additional exemption, such as that made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, would overcome the difficulties in the putting in of a system of combat pay or foreign service pay. I should like to discuss that matter with my officials and with the service authorities, and see what the implications would be, before I attempt to take any firm decision on it. But that is my position. I want to do what is fair and just for the service personnel, and for the people of Canada as a whole. By the necessary discussion here, I think we can probably arrive at what that policy should be. But I deeply appreciate the tone that the debate has taken this afternoon. There has been nothing controversial in it, in the sense of party controversy; and I know that we can keep the discussion on that basis.
Just in case the minister should attach any significance to what he pointed out as being the lack of expression of views by veterans-

I give this suggestion to the minister. He has been good in this debate. He has given us an opportunity to speak. In fact, he has invited comment on this matter. I may tell him that the effect of this $6.85 on the morale of the barrack room will be most serious. That seems to me to be the important point, not whether a private soldier, or sergeant or W.O. should pay $6.85 or whatever the amount is. There is this fact to be considered. When you are sitting in a room or tent or hole, sometime you are going to start discussing this matter with someone else; and in the barrack room-as these things always are-the thing becomes magnified until you come to the end of the month and then the boys are all dissatisfied. That is not the way to do it. It is not just a matter of $6.85. It is a matter of morale. Do not charge those fellows $6.85 a month for income tax. You cannot do that and at the same time maintain morale; because some barrack room lawyer, talking to a bunch of privates during the week, is going to kick this thing in the face and you are going to have a lot of trouble. That is the important point, to my mind; not whether a private soldier has to pay tax, but whether he should pay it on the basis of morale. As I got up in the army a little bit I found out what officers think about income tax. I never did have much respect for second lieutenants and lieutenants, but so far as the ranks above that are concerned, I think they could well afford to pay their income tax. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is the section relating to related companies. The law now provides that only one of a group of related corporations may receive the benefit of the lower rate of 15 per cent on the first $10,000 of income. Corporations are considered to be related if 70 per cent or more of the common shares of each of them are owned by one person, or a group of persons, or by persons not dealing with each other at arm's length. By definition persons are not dealing with each other at arm's length if connected by blood relationship, marriage or adoption. As a result, under the law as it now stands a corporation owned by one brother in Montreal and a corporation owned by another brother in Vancouver have been considered to be related although they may each be carrying on an entirely different line of business and be separate in every way. It is proposed to relieve this situation by providing that corporations controlled by persons not dealing at arm's length be not considered as related unless one of the persons owns shares in the capital stock of both corporations.

As it appears from a first reading of this paragraph, one would think that possibly the definition of related corporations was going to be made to depend upon the question of whether or not the same person owned shares in both companies. That is what it looks like here, and there is a question I should like to ask. Is there going to be any change in the definition so that if a person happens to own shares in both companies it will then make them related corporations as the result of the wording in this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A person is not dealing at arm's length in that circumstance. We had a number of cases brought to our attention. I cited the example of the two brothers. I had one case brought to my attention of two brothers-and sometimes this happens in families-who were not even speaking to each other and had not for years. They were 80709-203

both in business with their own corporations. Under the definition contained in the act they were related corporations, and only one of them could get the benefit of the $10,000 exemption. Needless to say there was considerable difficulty in arriving at a decision as to who would get the benefit of the exemption. That was not the sort of thing that the law was intended to prevent. It is obvious that the restrictions are intended to prevent people splitting up larger businesses in order to get the benefit of the lower exemption. I think we have progressively improved the definition. This represents the result of a good deal of consideration and, I think, achieves an equitable result without involving any risk of tax evasion.

Let me put the question I have for the minister by way of an example. The last three lines of the resolution read:
. . . so as not to include in the class of related corporations those controlled by persons not dealing at arm's length unless such persons own shares in the capital stock of both corporations.
At first it would seem that might widen the relationship as to when they would not be deemed to be related. However, let us take two companies that are not doing the same type of business but Mr. X happens to own one share in each corporation. Here you have a case of a person who owns a share of the capital stock of both corporations. The point I am worried about is whether it is going to be the result of this resolution that that fact will make them related corporations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not sure that I have followed my hon. friend quite as well as I should, but at present persons are deemed to be not dealing at arm's length if they are, as I said, connected by blood relationship, marriage or adoption. Therefore only one corporation owned by that family group would be eligible for exemption. As a result of the proposed amendment, if one brother owns all the shares in one company, another brother owns all the shares in another, the father owns the shares in a third, a sister owns the shares in a fourth, and another brother owns the shares in a fifth, they can all be considered as independent companies for the purpose of the $10,000 exemption provided none of them has any shares in any of the others. Then the other factor to determine whether the companies are related will be that one person must still own more than 70 per cent of the shares?

The point I tried to make a year ago and which I shall try to make again is that in some parts of this country, where people live at great distances from medical attention or hospitals, often the actual incidental expenses necessary to obtain medioal attention are much higher in proportion than the medical expenses themselves. speechtext:
Perhaps I could say a brief
word, Mr. Chairman, on this paragraph and the two succeeding ones. The amendments to be founded on these paragraphs will extend for another year the concessions now allowed for exploration expenses in the mining, oil and gas industry and will assure the exemption of the first three years of income of any new metalliferous or industrial mineral mine that comes into production before the end of 1954.

It is a rather curious thing
that the only natural resources receiving these special exemptions are oil, gas or mining and exploring for minerals. These commodities, of course, produce a great deal less revenue than the most important thing we have in Canada, our forest resources. I have been a rather patient soul, since I have been waiting for a number of years to hear that some consideration had been given to our forest resources. Always the government was considering this problem or giving it careful study. That has been going on for six years. While I know there have been many problems that the government has faced and solved in that time, I am afraid that they have put this forestry problem down at the bottom of the heap. Evidently they thought there was no necessity for giving it consideration.
As the minister will agree, our forests are our greatest source of revenue from a taxation point of view. They probably have the greatest potential value for the future. We are going to have forests today and forests tomorrow. I think we can guarantee that

Income Tax Act
the minister is going to get a substantial part of his revenue from the forests as long as Canada is here. The way the matter stands now, a taxpayer can deduct his expenses so far as forestry and silviculture are concerned on the particular piece of property from which he is taking logs at the present time. No incentive at all is given to any of our great forestry corporations, large or small, to try to provide a supply of wood for the future. As a matter of fact, the government seems to have a negative approach to the whole question. They say, "Yes, we realize it is a desirable thing that forests be put on a sustained yield basis." But on the other hand, they do not give any encouragement at all to people to invest money in growing trees. I am wondering whether there is any possibility of the minister giving some definite consideration to this problem within the next year, with a view to encouraging people to invest their money in growing timber.

Mr. Chairman, I felt that

The situation is that this corporation has ceased to carry on the wide functions it carried on last year and up until the end of the last fiscal year, as the procurement agency for the armed services. It is now left with the function of being a procurement agent for certain other countries, for their purchases in Canada in some fields; that is, the purchases may or may not go through this corporation.
For instance, as is well known, base metals are purchased in Canada by other countries directly from the companies concerned. But in other types of direct defence production, purchases would go through the Canadian Commercial Corporation. In order to illustrate just how sharp was the reduction, I indicated that the staff had been reduced from about 660 to about 40. Its function is as described by the leader of the opposition, namely, the purchasing agency for foreign governments in Canada.
There is one minor limitation on that description. Certain bulk purchases of one or two materials that may be made for Canadian account would continue to go through it. As hon. members will appreciate, I am referring to one or two strategic materials. They might be purchased through Canadian Commercial Corporation. But with that exception, there is no purchasing for the Canadian defence department through this corporation. I think that clarifies the point raised by the leader of the opposition.

Latest move by Stanley Knowles (C.C.F.-Winnipeg North Centre) to try and get divorce courts set up in Quebec and Newfoundland is his effort to have both houses of parliament deal with divorce suits from these provinces individually, instead of in batches as at present. I have read with interest many reports in newspapers in all parts of the country and I have heard radio broadcasts with respect to this matter and, except for these two instances, universally the point has been caught and made clear by the press and by radio reporters that what I am seeking support for in the house is that divorce cases should be transferred from parliament to a federal court here in the city of Ottawa.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are a
few particulars about this case of which I think the committee should be aware. In the first place it is noted that the petitioner is the husband and he is a private in the Canadian army. I am glad to note that the Senate committee recommended the remission of at least a part of the fees required in the other place in view of the difficult circumstances in which this man finds himself. It appears that there are two children, and that at the time the application was
Private Bills-Divorce made before the Senate they were in the custody of the father and were staying with his mother. He indicated that the wife had access to visit them but of course he is supporting the children.
He said in the course of his evidence that he was not supporting his wife. If the evidence of adultery in this case is valid I certainly do not blame this man for not supporting his wife. Where is this place called Rawdon? It seems to have been the scene of the adultery, and I notice that it is named in a number of these cases as the place where the evidence is obtained. Again, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that parliament should be aware of the seriousness of the job that we are undertaking in dealing with these matters. This is indeed a sad case. This wife and mother has run out on her soldier husband and two children. Again it seems to me it is the kind of case that should have been dealt with in a court.

This is one of the cases in which I am interested because of the fact that there are children involved. One is four years of age and the other two. These little children are left to the mercy of people who were not able to get along in their marriage. That is an unsatisfactory situation, because no one knows who is to take care of them. In the meantime we are told they are in the custody of the mother of the father of the children, but that the wife who, according to the decision of the Senate, is the guilty party, also has access to them. I suggest to you, sir, that quite outside of the merits of the case there is a nasty situation. The two little children, one four and one two, are just getting to the stage where they can begin to recognize and love their parents. Yet nobody knows who owns them and nobody knows who is to take care of them. There will probably be another battle between the parents as to who will have custody of them.
That is one of the reasons why I suggested the other night that I thought it was a foolish procedure to have a court as at present constituted, which, while it has the responsibility and the authority to dissolve a marriage, apparently deliberately takes the position, as I read in a case the other night, that it has no responsibility in the matter of the custody of children. So far as I am concerned, that is the main interest that I have in this and similar cases. I would say that in this case the home is already broken up irreparably, but there is one thing that can be done. The lives of these little children can be salvaged. I suggest that the method by which they can be salvaged is to have a properly constituted federal court under

Private Bills-Divorce whose jurisdiction the business of such salvage would come. At the present time these little children are being sent from pillar to post without parents, without anybody, taking any interest in them.
I think the responsibility in this matter falls upon us. That is why I said the other night that, so far as I am concerned, if we are going to do this work we should do it carefully and well, from now on scrutinizing each case in the short time at our disposal. There is not much time available. It is a scramble to get the evidence read in time to be able to speak about it. I think we should resolve from now on that if the House of Commons is a divorce court we shall have to carry out our duty as best we can in view of the responsibility which we owe to the people who sent us here as well as to these parents and children. I am quite certain that the people who sent me here did not send me to be a judge in a divorce court.

In this case I should like to point out something similar to what I pointed out the other evening in respect to another case, and I shall read a little of the evidence here. It is in respect to whether or not the marriage certificate issued by the officiating clergyman is proof of marriage. Mr. Phillips was the solicitor in this case and he asked the witness this question:
Q. I show you a marriage certificate giving the details of your marriage. Is that a true record of your marriage?
A. Yes, sir.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Who is that signed by, Vatcher?
Yes, by the officiating minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
You haven't one from the superior court?
There was no reply to that. The chairman then asked:
Q. This is the one you received from the minister at the time of the marriage?
A. Yes, sir.
The only evidence they had to prove this marriage was the certificate the clergyman had given them, and that is not usually accepted as proof of a marriage. The reason for that is that you can go to a book store and buy marriage certificates. You can tear marriage certificates out of family bibles. Such a certificate could be signed by Reverend John Smith of Timbuctoo and palmed off as a marriage certificate. The document that is proof of marriage is an abstract of the registration of that marriage; and the marriage is not registered until the official documents other than marriage certificates are made out and registered with the proper authorities in the various provinces. Upon the registration of that marriage one may obtain an abstract of that registration. That


is accepted as proof of marriage, because the officiating clergyman signing the certificate must be licensed by the province.
I am not arguing against this case, for the reason that the wife of the man applying for the divorce testified herself, and on her evidence I believe the application should be granted. I just point out that an ordinary marriage certificate given by a clergyman is not necessarily legal proof that a couple are married.

I wonder if the sponsor of this bill, the hon. member for Lisgar, can say how much time was spent on this case by the committee on miscellaneous private bifis.
Mf. Winkler: I believe this bill was dealt with in bulk with a number of others.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am not surprised at that answer, because that is the way most of them are dealt with as far as the committee on miscellaneous private bills is concerned. It is clear that the case was given fairly ample consideration in the Senate because the evidence runs to fifteen pages, which is a little more than the average of the books of evidence that come to our desks.
After reading this evidence I acknowledge the job the members of the Senate committee do. I have no quarrel with them and no reflection to cast upon the way they do their work. My whole point is that they should not be asked to do it, just as we should not be asked; and I am sure they would like, as we would, to be rid of the whole matter.
This case appears to be another of war's tragedies. This couple were married in 1937 and appear to have lived together quite happily for a number of years. They had one child. The husband enlisted and went overseas, and it appears that after a while his letters to his wife became infrequent and a bit unfriendly. She suspected that he must have formed another attachment overseas, but she had no evidence to that effect and it was her hope that their marriage was

still intact. However, when he came back to Canada at the end of the war he got in touch with his wife and indicated that it was not his intention to live with her. It was not long after that before the wife lost all track of her husband, and she had to do her best to support herself and her child. As a matter of fact from the time he came home after the war until August, 1950, the husband did not contribute anything to the support of his child.
Sometime before 1950 this wife learned that her husband was living in Belleville, Ontario, with another woman. Indeed the information that reached her was that he and the other woman had another child and that they were living together in Belleville as a family. On learning that, this lady took steps to obtain a divorce from her husband. Before doing so she had applied to the Ontario courts at Belleville and obtained an order compelling this man to pay $25 a month for the support of his child. I am wondering just what happens to that court order once this divorce goes through. I do not find anything in the evidence to indicate what will happen to it, but in the absence of any question being raised by the senators who made up this committee I dare to hope that this man will be required to continue that payment of $25 a month for the support of his child.
To get back to the story of what this soldier did after he got back to Canada, as I say he got in touch with his wife and indicated that he did not wish to live with her any more. Later it appears that he was instrumental in persuading the Canadian immigration authorities to bring to Canada the girl whose name is Betty. Her last name seems not to be known, but she came from England. It is this girl with whom he is living at Belleville. Now, the evidence seems to be fairly clear. It seems to me it is evidence not only of adultery, but it is evidence of the first marriage having been dissolved by the action of the husband in going off and living with another woman and starting to raise another family.
Hon. members will recognize-
May I ask a question at this point?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: -that I recite these facts with nothing but sorrow. The whole story is a sad one, and everyone will feel-
I rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: -that it is a tragedy.
