The house in committee on Bill No. 122, for the relief of Marie Blanche Amilda Lessard Duplessis-Mr. Winkler-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-Marriage dissolved.

The other night, in talking about this matter, I cast some doubt upon the integrity of investigators. If we consider some of the bills before us here, I believe we shall come to the conclusion that a lot of these investigators make their money simply by this, what I consider, nefarious trade. My friend refers to it as a "racket" and I shall agree with him to that extent, but I would rather have my own phraseology. In the preceding bill, one might have noticed that the lady involved was unknown, except in so far as her first name was concerned. Apparently these investigators could not find out her second name. They could find out everything else, but they just knew her first name. There was no other name in the

evidence, and no one knows what the lady's maiden name was. I come now to this Bill No. 122 which concerns a certain lady by the name of Duplessis residing in Montreal, who sues for divorce from her husband. It is sad to note that this marriage took place in 1921, almost thirty years ago. Now, we have a divorce case.
I was speaking, sir, about the integrity, or lack of it, of these investigators. I should like to draw to your attention that in this particular case the alleged adultery upon which the verdict was given was committed with an unknown woman in the city of Montreal. Now, sir, these investigators were able to find out everything else but were unable to ascertain the name of this woman. I believe, sir, it is a fact that some of these investigators are not as straightforward as they might be. I am going to suggest that these women can be obtained for the particular purpose of supplying evidence in these particular cases. There is a conviction in many quarters that a good many of these cases are the result of collusion and that the evidence at times is faked. I think that matter should be brought to the attention of the public.
May I say that the public knows nothing about these divorce bills. The public does not know to what extent we in the House of Commons are crucified by the study of these divorce cases, to say nothing of the senators in the other place. I think it is a good thing that it should be on the record of the House of Commons that one or two members at least, among whom I am one, believe that many of these cases are the result of collusion, the result of faked evidence which is deliberately obtained by the sort of investigators, lawyers and witnesses that we have in some of these cases. When I say that, I am casting no aspersions on the profession that I have named, because I am well aware of the fact that a reputable lawyer would have nothing to do with that kind of thing.
But there is the position as I see it. Some of these cases are those in regard to which I think there may be some suspicion. It is too facile, too easy to be able to go out and get divorce evidence. I am told that in certain cases you can go to these people, and you do not have to do anything. They simply provide the evidence. They provide everything. The whole thing is arranged and that is the end of it. It is disgusting but it is true, in my opinion.

There are just one or two things I should like to bring out in connection with this bill and which I think might be of some value to members of the committee. In the first place, may I say that I

have found some difficulty in being able to determine the difference between connivance and collusion. This is one case in which that difference appears to be explained. I should like to put this on Hansard; it is to be found at page 11 of this evidence. I should like to read it, with your permission, Mr. Chairman. Some little argument went on between the chairman and one of the solicitors in this case as to the meaning of these words. The solicitor said that he always understood "connivance" and "collusion" to be synonymous terms. The chairman, Mr. Aseltine, a man who has given some considerable study to this matter, puts him right on this particular point. He says no, that there is a difference in the meaning; and he pulls out a volume, I suppose by Power, because that is what he reads; and this is what he says:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Power on Divorce. It deals with collusion, connivance and condonance. It is the easiest thing in the world to study. For instance, if a woman arranged to have her husband found by detectives under certain circumstances-
That would be collusion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That would be connivance, she
was arranging the evidence. Collusion is an arrangement between them. To give you an example, after you commenced an' action she could go to her husband, and arrange not to have a contestation.

That would be both collusion and
connivance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Or that she give him something.
That is collusion.
And it is connivance too.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
No, you only connive at the
adultery.
That throws some light on that particular point. There is another matter, Mr. Chairman, that I should like to bring to your attention. I have always wondered how much it might cost these people to go through the process of obtaining a divorce; and I find that here that information is brought out. The witness is asked by the solicitor:
Q. How much have you paid now? A. $800, I think.
Q. $800? A. Yes.
Q. Does that include the full parliamentary fees paid, $210?
The Clerk of the Committee:	Yes, it has been
paid, Mr. Chairman.
Looking at this particular case, I feel that that is a great deal of money to pay for what this man got.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This woman.

For what this woman got, I should say. It is a woman in this case. Her husband had been actually living with the other woman for about a year. Even the chairman makes the remark

perhaps I had better read it to you. It is to be found at page 13 of the evidence:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

I don't know why you want to
hire detectives in a case like this, why didn't you take your client and go down there yourself?

It was only a matter of going there and finding that they were living there as man and wife; and they had been living there for about a year. Yet it cost this woman about $800. Perhaps that is cheap; I do not know. Some costs may run a great deal higher than that. But that is a great deal of money. I think the chairman of this committee is to be commended for calling that matter to the attention of the solicitors. I think the Senate committee that handles these cases are humane, and that they are to be commended for that action.
There is one other point in this evidence that I do not like, and I will read it to you. This investigator goes into this room, turns on the light and commences to say what he saw; and he says "An old woman-". Then Senator Howden rather butts in and asks the question: "Q. An old-?"; and before he can say anything else the investigator says:
A. An old lady, she looked to be fifty or fifty-five.
I do not like that. I do not call a lady of fifty or fifty-five an old lady or an old woman. Many of them look quite young at that age. Besides, if that is so, how old does that make me? Perhaps the investigator could be a little bit more careful in his appraisal of the age of the fair sex.

Q. And you continued to live with your sister and you still do? A. Yes, sir.

Q. And your sister looks after your child? A. Yes.

She earns $25 a week working in a restaurant in Montreal as a cashier. We sometimes hear of cases where cashiers are accused of theft, and when you consider

I am quite ready to admit that a transfer of the matter to the exchequer court probably would not help in this particular, but in my opinion the whole matter of divorce, particularly as it affects children in these cases, should be gone into very thoroughly; because we have an obligation not only to the innocent party but to any children of the marriage. I am pointing out that it is impossible for this woman to bring up this child properly herself and maintain her appearance as a cashier when the wages are as low as those she gave to the Senate committee as having been received.

And Mr. Golden and I forced our way into the room.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at six
o'clock we were discussing paragraph (d) of section 3 and I had indicated that this amendment was intended to clarify the power of the corporation because of a legal doubt that had been raised as to its authority. The leader of the opposition had asked what was the act to which this doubt referred, and what was the doubt. The act to which the doubt referred arose in connection with the purchase of some wool stock. There was no doubt raised as to the right to buy wool outside of Canada, but a legal question was raised as to the right to pay for wool bought within Canada; it was as to that part of the transaction that doubt was raised.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Would that power not be given by paragraph (c) which gives the corporation the power to exercise on behalf and under the direction of the minister any powers or functions vested in the minister by any other act that authorizes the minister to employ the
Canadian Commercial Corporation corporation to exercise them? Would that not be broad enough to enable the corporation to do this purchasing?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Apparently not. The purchase of the wool was authorized under what was then the Essential Materials (Defence) Act and a question was raised as to the payment for the part purchased in Canada out of funds of the Canadian Commercial Corporation under the other section. The hon. member has put his finger on the point. It was thought that paragraph (c) was wide enough and that the authority in the other act to use the Canadian Commercial Corporation to carry out the functions authorized by the other act would be wide enough. Apparently there was a question raised beyond that. As I made clear earlier, I found it difficult to concede that there was legal doubt, but that is the situation that has developed.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
May I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that there would seem to be a rather dangerous principle introduced by the latter part of this paragraph (d). The first part of paragraph (d) gives the Canadian Commercial Corporation the power to exercise any function conferred on it by any other act. If some other act sets out that the Canadian Commercial Corporation can do certain things, the corporation can carry on accordingly. But the latter part of this paragraph (d) seems to confer wide-open authority to do anything without parliamentary sanction and without any act referring to the corporation. It says:
-or for the exercise of which it may be employed under any other act.
The key word is "employed". That means that a minister administering any other act may decide to employ the Canadian Commercial Corporation, and that would be permitted under the latter part of this paragraph. Surely that is contrary to the whole intent of the act and is against parliamentary principles because there is no parliamentary check. In other words, broad power is being given here without any definition by parliament at all, power for other ministers to use this corporation. I think that is most unwise and is going too far.
It looks to me as though in trying to widen this power the officials have gone too far. It would not be the first time they have done that because they like to make sure that there is sufficient power in an act. Quite often they do not seem to think about the powers being excessive, but I suggest that here is a case where excessive powers are being sought.

Canadian Commercial Corporation

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with due
deference to the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra I must say that the interpretation which he places on the latter part of the paragraph is much too wide. It simply provides that the corporation may exercise powers for the exercise of which it may be employed under any other act. There must be authority under another act to employ the Canadian Commercial Corporation. But having employed the corporation as agent to procure materials this paragraph makes it clear that the other powers granted in the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act can be used. For example, there would be the right under section 8 to use funds of the corporation. It has that much narrower interpretation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: The parliamentary assistant interprets these words as meaning that there must be some other act which actually sets out that the Canadian Commercial Corporation can be employed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: If that is what it means, that meets my objection.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Some other act or some other legislation having granted the right to use the corporation, then the corporation can use all the provisions of its own act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: The parliamentary assistant means that the Canadian Commercial Corporation cannot be employed by any other department or any other crown company unless there is an act which actually sets out that it can be employed by that branch or agency of government?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: That is right; there has to be the other authority. Of course there is the earlier section which we are not amending about exports and imports. Perhaps I could revert for a moment to the act that caused the difficulty. It was a matter of payment, not the authority to be employed as the agent; it was the question of using the funds of Canadian Commercial Corporation to make payment for part of the wool which had been bought in Canada. I admit it seems to be a refined argument. The hon. member will realize that lawyers differ, and I thought it was an over-refined objection. However, there it was.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think any of us want to split hairs in regard to the interpretation of this section, but like the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra I feel that there is a dangerous tendency to try to cure imaginary or uncertain troubles by simply saying, "Well, all right, we will put in something wide enough so that there


will be no chance that it will not deal with everything that may arise." The parliamentary assistant was good enough between six o'clock and the time we resumed discussion of this bill to indicate some of the considerations that had led to the inclusion of this amendment. However, I would point out to him that there' is one act in connection with which it is not necessary for the Canadian Commercial Corporation to be designated and in which there are wide powers. Under the Emergency Powers Act there is almost limitless power to set up any type of organization by order in council and then designate the Canadian Commercial Corporation as the agency for carrying out that particular function. One reason why I feel it is very unsatisfactory to put in a wide-open provision of this kind is because it is quite frankly stated in the explanatory notes on the opposite page that the purpose is to take care of any powers conferred upon it which are not specifically covered by its present designated powers. That would mean that, while at the present time Canadian Commercial Corporation has certain designated powers under the act which brought it into existence, and while under other statutes such as the Defence Production Act there would be some general limitation as to the nature of the activities that could be covered, under the Emergency Powers Act activities in no way contemplated by the general purpose of the Defence Production Act or the general designated purpose of this act could be carried forward, and then Canadian Commercial Corporation would be deemed to have powers for such purpose.
That might seem to be creating imaginary problems, but I believe the time has come when, unless there is some very clearly stated reason, we should hesitate to give these blanket powers under any statute. I do not want to labour the matter unduly but I would point out that the Emergency Powers Act passed during this session was passed with the statement that in the first place it repealed the emergency act passed last September and conferred wider powers on the government so that the powers might be wide enough to introduce price controls. That was the reason stated. The government needed no wider powers to establish priorities, to stockpile or to do any of the things contemplated from the point of view of positive control and allocation of supplies, but it was stated by the minister who assumed responsibility both for the drafting and the argument in support of the bill that the wider bill was needed so that the government might deal with price controls.
We have come this far in the session and the government has still given no indication

that it has any thought of exercising the one authority for which it obtained wider powers. With that as an example I suggest that we should not give wide powers like these without specific information as to why they are needed, and not just a general statement that somebody may have some doubt about some wool contract. For that reason I move:
That subsection (d) of section 3 be deleted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there may
be a question of order as to moving the deletion of a section, but leaving that aside for the moment and reverting to the argument, if the Emergency Powers Act is as wide in its authority as the leader of the opposition says it is then of course orders passed under it can re-enact any of the clauses asked for here. I submit that argument is wholly irrelevant to the section we are discussing. The section under consideration has to do with a situation stated clearly in the explanatory note referred to by the leader of the opposition. The note reads in part:
. . . and second, to resolve the legal doubt raised as to whether the corporation may exercise a power not included among its specified purposes.
Under section 4 of the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act the specified purpose in the wool contract related to the right to import wool, and the only other section dealing with powers was part II of the act which had to do with materials for the defence department. The wool purchase did not come directly and squarely within either of these two specified purposes in the Canadian Commercial Corporation legislation. Therefore we had an extraordinary situation where we were seeking to buy wool for defence purposes to provide uniforms- and I think properly seeking to do so-and we could pay for wool bought in other countries but could not pay for wool bought in Canada. The purpose is to clear up that sort of situation. The authority to buy wool of course arises from the essential materials legislation.

speechtext:
Would not the very fact that

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.

passed which specifically states that the Canadian Commercial Corporation may do certain things, surely that is sufficient without then amending the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act to say it can do the things that the other act has said it can do. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: I suppose the answer to that would be to bring before the house all the other legislation authorizing the use of the Canadian Commercial Corporation, amend each section giving that authority and put it in the widest possible language, but this amendment makes it clear that the Canadian Commercial Corporation has, if authorized under other legislation, full capacity to act as authorized.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: Is not sufficient. We are back now on the argument that caused the doubt. speechtext:

Canadian Commercial Corporation we do? I have not found the law officers of the crown infallible. After all, they are only there to advise, but their opinion is not necessarily correct and need not necessarily be accepted. Here they have taken a pile driver to drive a tack. They have taken far wider power than is necessary to meet the situation which is worrying them. I suggest that the parliamentary assistant should accept the amendment of the leader of the opposition. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra quite overstated my position. I did not assert that I either give the time, or have the opportunity to give the time, or at the moment think it perhaps desirable that the time be given, to a study of some of the more intricate legal arguments raised from day to day on a great many matters. I for one find it desirable and necessary to take the opinions of competent legal men in the various departments on their own work. I find it a very good rule to follow that, if you nave an expert whom you trust, you should take his opinion. If you do not trust him .then perhaps he should not be employed.
I am asked why I do not accept the amendment and leave out this section. The answer is that very shortly we would be right back in the situation in which we found ourselves previously. A short time ago we had to buy wool. We found that we could not pay for any wool bought in Canada, though we could pay for wool bought in other parts of the world, which was a most extraordinary position. This section clears up that difficulty; but I suggest it is not a wide section, and that the proper method is to amend this act to make it clear that the Canadian Commercial Corporation, if authorized by any other legislation, has the right to use all the powers given it under its own act. For that reason I have no alternative but to regretfully reject the amendment of the leader of the opposition.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
This section does give the minister fairly comprehensive powers. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. I know these legal arguments in regard to the interpretation of acts and the breadth of amending sections may seem at times very boring and like a waste of time. I would recall, however, that step by step we have been seeing the powers of parliament whittled away by the extension of wider and wider powers through amendments or whole new acts, in which very little definite information is given beyond the fact that someone thinks powers of this kind might be needed. I refer again to the Emergency Powers Act passed earlier this session, which gives this government the widest powers ever conferred upon any democratic government except in time of general war. Those powers were extended by the majority vote of this parliament with practically nothing before this house to demonstrate the need for powers of that kind.
As I pointed out earlier the one reason, the only clear reason, given for the extension of such powers was that it was necessary to make the earlier emergency powers still

wider so the government could deal with price controls. There were general statements as to the need for stand-by powers; there was the statement that many of the things the government might require to do would never become necessary as long as sweeping powers of this kind were available, which those who might be affected would know might be exercised. Those powers are there. I would point out that under those powers there is no question, and none has ever been suggested, but that the government could by order in council-and this is merely an example-take over the operation of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: A good idea.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: What has that to do with this bill?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not going to be diverted by comments so ridiculous as those just made. If the hon. member who made that remark had any understanding of the extent of the experience, to say nothing of the efficiency, of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario, he would not make an utterly silly and irrelevant comment of that kind.
That could be done. I ask the parliamentary assistant if he would question the proposition that if such an order were made, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce said in the earlier discussion of this subject it could be made, the Canadian Commercial Corporation could then be appointed as agent to operate it. I have used that only as an illustration. The same thing could be done to take over all the operating oil fields of Alberta, or to take over the iron development in Labrador. It could be done to take over any other operation regarded by. the government as something that was needed for the general welfare of Canada during a period of emergency, which was the basis for the act that was passed earlier in the session.
That being so, Mr. Chairman, I simply repeat that this house in committee is disregarding the responsibilities of parliament if, without anything more than a general statement that somebody thinks they need powers of this kind to deal with a wool contract, we should confer powers so wide, when at the very time the amending bill is before us the parliamentary assistant says he does not believe it is actually necessary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: He did not say that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Surely at some point this house must say it is not going to accord the government further and wider powers simply to resolve doubts, when the specific case can be dealt with if necessary by an amendment to the section of the act under which these
Canadian Commercial Corporation powers were conferred. The Canadian Commercial Corporation was given very wide powers when it was brought into being by an act passed on August 31, 1946. Simply to illustrate why I am taking objection to the extension of wider powers with nothing more before us than we have at the moment, let me read section 4 which designates the purposes of the corporation:
(1) The corporation is established for the following purposes:
(a)	to assist in the development of trade between Canada and other nations, and
(b)	to assist persons in Canada
(1)	to obtain goods and commodities from outside Canada; and
(ii) to dispose of goods and commodities that are available for export from Canada.
(2)	The corporation shall comply with any general or special direction given by the governor in council or the minister with reference to carrying out its purposes.
Then, it goes on in section 5 to say:
5. (X) The corporation may do such things as it deems expedient for, or conducive to, the attainment of the purposes set forth in section four of this act; and, for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing, the corporation may carry on the business of:
(a)	importing goods or commodities into Canada, and
(b)	exporting goods or commodities from Canada, either as principal or as agent, in such manner and to such extent as it deems advisable to achieve the said purposes.
(2) The generality of subsection one of this section is not restricted by any provision of this act other than section four thereof.
Now, Mr. Chairman, with these wide powers which cover every aspect of the activities which the ministerial assistant has stated this corporation now requires, I suggest that there is no occasion to pass an amendment which extends powers beyond those wide powers; and that those powers, as conferred by the act itself, conform fully with what we have been told the act is now going to be called upon to do. I repeat that the explanation of the object of the amending section, written in by those who drafted the legislation, says-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Frankly I had hoped it was,
because I had hoped it was drafted by those who knew what the purpose was. I take the correction. These words are put in perhaps by someone else, but whoever wrote them, the words which are supposed to explain the amendment as written on the left-hand pages say:
... to resolve the legal doubt raised as to whether the corporation may exercise a power not included among its specified purposes.
It means only one thing, namely that the intention of this amendment is to give to the Canadian Commercial Corporation powers

Canadian Commercial Corporation not covered by these designated powers passed by parliament. I suggest again, Mr. Chairman, that with the statement of the parliamentary assistant that, in his opinion, it is not needed, without any specific legal argument to show why it is needed, parliament should not pass a power of this kind. Therefore I close my remarks with the hope that on this occasion an amendment of this kind may not be pressed so that parliament itself can, at least on this occasion, assert its authority to control legislation until it knows exactly why something should be done.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: These objections are raised in the best of faith in the belief that this section is too broad. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant would have no objection to letting this bill stand over the week end, and have it considered further by the experts.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.

No, I think there is every objection to that. We have had some questions about the defence production department awarding contracts in various parts of the country. I should very much like to answer that specious argument that is being put forward rather regularly, taut this is neither the occasion nor, in my opinion, is it within the rules to deal with it here. I must say I would rather welcome the opportunity to deal with it.
Then we got into another discussion about the wisdom or lack of wisdom of taking over the Ontario hydro, and about how well run the Ontario hydro was. I also have some views about that, but I do not think this is the place or the occasion for me to express them.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt, but I would point out that I did not raise this subject. I simply raised this as an example, because the minister himself had on an earlier occasion said that this act had sufficiently wide powers for that purpose.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.

speechtext: That is self-evident.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, it is self-evident. It is one of those things I believe one should learn very early in life. I do not know that it is proper for one member to say to another member that he does not know anything

about this subject or that. He may or he may not. I have an idea that all members know a great deal about a great many subjects, and I have never been tempted to take the attitude that other members do not know anything about the subject under discussion. I do not believe in that point of view.
In any event, that is not the point before the chair. At the moment, the point is rather narrow, ahd it concerns paragraph (d) of section 3. The leader of the opposition makes some such remark as, "Let's start asking questions". I should like to be permitted to continue my argument without a lot of questions about this or that. The leader of the opposition correctly read sections 4 and 5 of the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act. It will be noted that these sections deal exclusively with export or import. This power is being taken, to clear up a difficulty that arose in another part of the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act having to do with the procurement of defence supplies. It was thought that the power in that legislation providing for the use of the capital made available to Canadian Commercial Corporation for making temporary payment of purchases would be sufficient in certain circumstances, but that was found not to be so.
I did not take the position that paragraph (d) of section 3 was not necessary. It is necessary, otherwise I would not have come here with the paragraph in the bill asking hon. members to approve it. The paragraph reads:
(d) to exercise any other powers or functions conferred upon it by any other act or for the exercise of which it may be employed under any other act.
Now, we had an' experience where this corporation was employed under another act in its proper function of procuring raw wool supplies. The point was raised that, having been employed to buy this wool, it could only buy the wool from other countries under the very sections read by the hon. leader of the opposition. It was found that the corporation did not have the power to pay for wool bought in Canada. Do hon. members want the corporation left in the position of having to buy only from foreign countries? If it is to pay for the goods itself, that is what happens. It can buy in Canada if it is not paying for the goods itself. Do hon. members want that situation to continue? I suggest the amendment is as simple as that, and I suggest the amendment is as narrow as that.
I indicated earlier the functions of the corporation, which are now much narrower than they were. Its only function now being

performed where this situation would arise at all would be in certain types of bulk purchases, of which there are very few. To leave ourselves in the position where the corporation could not use its own capital to make certain emergency bulk purchases is not what the members of the committee want.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope we can deal with this matter without an attempt
Canadian Commercial Corporation to set up a straw man, as was done with regard to an illustration that was used simply to try to clarify the extent of the activities that would be embraced by such an amendment as this, because that has some bearing on whether an amendment of this kind is necessary. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO PERMIT PERFORMANCE OF SERVICES FOR DEPARTMENT OF DEFENCE PRODUCTION, ETC.
speechtext: As a matter of fact, the act is automatically superseded by the act which was passed at this session; and the powers conferred now are much wider than those which were made available under the other act. Therefore it seems-and in that I was under the impression that the parliamentary assistant shared that view, from what he said earlier this evening in this committee- that it would be possible to deal with this contract in that particular way. But even if it were not, that could be dealt with by a specific amendment. But now we are asked to extend these powers to cases where they will go beyond the specified purposes of the Canadian Commercial Corporation, as approved by this parliament. We ought to know what it is we are doing; because this power is not to be limited to this one case; this is a wide general power to engage in activities not covered by the purposes established by parliament. If we are going to do that, then I suggest that we should know something of the scale of the activities. For that reason I think we should know exactly how many contracts have been executed by the Canadian Commercial Corporation which are now being handled by that corporation, and what the value of those contracts is, so that we may know something of the scale of the business being done by the corporation which is being given these increased powers. Canadian Commercial Corporation Corporation Act. That is clear. That is the effect of this amendment; whereas previously, according to the explanatory note, it would not have been clear. I will take a concrete example.

Surely that is the effect of the explanatory note, and the original act, and the amendment which we are being called upon to pass. Before we leave the first item, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the representations that have been made to the government from time to time by various labour bodies, and by others who are interested, asking for the introduction of the principle of collective bargaining into the government service. As the minister knows,
I put a question on one aspect of this subject to the Secretary of State the other day. He did not give me an answer then, and I have been waiting hopefully for it day by day. The question I asked the Secretary of State was whether he was aware of the request of the Ontario Federation of Printing Trades Unions to the effect that the employees of the government printing bureau be accorded the right to collective bargaining. He told me he would answer in a few days, and I have a strong suspicion that when I get that answer it will be to the effect that as the legislation now stands there is no possibility of according collective bargaining rights to government employees in the federal printing bureau. Anticipating that I would get this answer from the Secretary of State I realized that my next question would have to be directed to the Minister of Labour, that I would have to ask him if consideration had been given to amending the federal labour code to provide that collective bargaining be accorded the printing bureau employees. Therefore, I assume we can take the answer of the Secretary of State as read, and so I move on to the next stage. Thus I am now putting the matter up to the Minister of Labour.
I feel very strongly that this matter should be considered. Indeed I feel there is a case for collective bargaining in many if not all the branches of the government service, -but I suggest that one -place it certainly could be started is in the federal printing bureau. It does not seem logical that employees of the Canadian National Railways, Trans-Canada Air Lines, Polymer Corporation and other bodies of that sort, which belong, to the government, should be permitted to organize and enter into collective bargaining with their employers while those in the printing bureau, which likewise belongs to the government, -are left in a different category. It seems to me that sooner or later this subject will have to be dealt with by the government as a

whole, but the person upon whose recommendation the government would make any move in this direction is the Minister of Labour, because the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act comes under his supervision. I draw to the attention of the minister the fact that two of the labour congresses, at any rate, which presented their briefs to the government this year-the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada and the Canadian Congress of Labour-asked for the right of collective bargaining for government employees.
I earnestly hope the minister is giving consideration to this matter. I realize that he has not been in the department very long, that he wants to get his feet, and get the feel of things in the labour field. But I can tell him there is a very strong feeling on the part of many government employees that this should be done. That certainly is the feeling over at the printing bureau. I want to be quite frank about this matter and say I am a member of the international typographical union, which means that I have contacts with many of the employees at the bureau and know how they feel about this matter. Similar representations from other government employees have been made to me, and I urge the minister to take appropriate steps.
That is perhaps the main point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister on this first item. One other matter I should like to draw to his attention is that in the two labour congress briefs to which I already have referred the minister and government are asked to include the check-off in the national labour code. The minister made some reference to this question in an earlier debate, as to whether or not labour really wanted the check-off in the code. I simply draw his attention to the fact that it was asked for again in the briefs of both these congresses. It was interesting to note that one of those congresses appeared before the government at about noon on April 10, asking amongst other things for the deductibility of trade union dues for income tax purposes. As the Minister of Labour recalls, that is one request that seemed to be granted in a hurry, because it was announced by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech that evening. It is good to know that some of these requests do get consideration, and I hope the minister will seriously consider the matters I have just drawn to his attention; that is, the question of collective bargaining rights for government employees, starting at the printing bureau and moving, I would hope, into other 80709-2041

A great deal has been made of the argument that unemployment insurance is not supposed to be a fund to provide for a honeymoon. It has been argued that if a woman who has been employed and contributing to the fund marries and quits her job, that is her business and she should not expect to draw unemployment insurance. But there are cases in which a married woman finds it necessary to work because her husband is not able to earn enough to make both ends meet at today's high prices. That woman is available for employment; she reports and wants to work but cannot get work, and is still denied her benefits because she has not proven her attachment to the labour market by being actually at work for 90 days after her marriage.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be glad to give consideration to that matter. On second thought, Mr. Chairman, I believe I should like to put on the record a statement regarding the married women's regulations before this general item is passed.
On November 15, 1950, the unemployment insurance commission made a regulation restricting the payment of benefits to married women. This regulation was designed to stop an unintended drain on the unemployment insurance fund through payments of benefit to married women who had really withdrawn from the labour market.
When the regulation had been in effect for a few months the commission made a survey of its local offices. This disclosed that during the first month after the regulation came into effect a large percentage of married women, whose claims were disallowed thereby, made no further effort to keep alive their applications for employment. Out of 8,884 married women who were disqualified because of this regulation during that period, approximately 18 per cent kept alive their application for employment; 5 per cent reported that they had found work; and 77 per cent allowed their application for employment to lapse.
The first few months of operation, and submissions to courts of referees, also disclosed

certain inequities. The commission proposed to make certain changes in the regulation, the principal amendments being: First, it was provided that the additional conditions imposed by the regulation would not apply to a married woman who left her employment voluntarily with just cause for reasons connected solely with her employment. This proviso was new, and was in addition to the other grounds on which a married woman claimant would not be subject to the regulation. Secondly, it was provided that the regulation would not apply to a married woman whose husband was wholly incapacitated for work for at least four consecutive weeks. The present provision is that the husband must be wholly and permanently incapacitated. However, the wife would not be relieved from having to fulfil the additional conditions imposed by the regulation if her husband was receiving compensation for the incapacity or was continuing to receive remuneration.
Before presenting these changes to the governor in council for approval the commission felt it desirable to consult representatives of the principal labour organizations. A meeting was held on April 10, 1951, to receive their views regarding proposed amendments, a draft of which had been circulated to these organizations beforehand. The organizations represented at the meeting were: The Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, Canadian Congress of Labour, the railway brotherhoods. The Canadian and Catholic Confederation of Labour was unable to send a representative but made known its views in writing.
In presenting the draft amendments for consideration by the unions, the commission pointed out that the result of this regulation, which came into effect November 15, 1950, amply justified the stand taken by the commission and the unemployment insurance advisory committee, and had proved conclusively that a large number of married women, who in the past have drawn benefit, were not actually in the labour market and were causing an undue drain on the fund.
The union representatives agreed that the amendments met many of their objections, but requested modification of two of the provisions as follows: The regulation provides that, to draw benefit, a married woman must be in employment for ninety days following marriage, if unemployed when married, or ninety days after the first separation from employment following marriage if she was employed when married. The unions asked that ninety days of employment should run from the date of marriage in either case. The commission felt that the adoption of this

suggestion would make the regulation of little value as a large number of women continue to work without any interruption for a considerable period after marriage. However, the commission is prepared to modify the regulation to the effect that if a married woman was in employment at the time of marriage only sixty of the ninety days of employment required be after the first separation after marriage. The unions objected to the provision that benefit would be denied a married woman while her husband was incapacitated if he was in receipt of compensation or remuneration while so incapacitated. The commission has expressed its willingness to delete this restriction from the regulation.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have a rather -complicated outline here which I would prefer not to put on the record at this time because, while this recommendation has been made by the chief commissioner to the minister, it has not been finally adopted by the governor in council, which is necessary to put the regulation into effect. I am quite -confident when that is done it will overcome the legitimate complaints that were made with regard to the married woman question.

agree that the drafting of that regulation leaves much to be desired. For a start, let me read section 5A (1). It is as follows:
Every married woman shall be diso.ualiiied from receiving benefits for the period of two years following her marriage unless she is relieved sooner from any such disqualification as provided in this section.
From reading that you would imagine that because a woman married, she immediately put herself outside the Unemployment Insurance Act. I am sure that was not intended; but that is exactly the interpretation that I would give this section. Then when you go on and find what has been added to that particular clause, while the minister's explanation that he read into the record sounds rather plausible, it certainly makes it exceedingly ambiguous and, in my opinion, does not change the thing at all. You would be led to believe that the reasonable thing to do would be to decide that if that woman retained her employment for sixty days, as is provided now in the proposed amendment, she would then be eligible for unemployment insurance. But that is not the case. In the second amendment to that particular section, it is definitely stated that she has to prove her right to unemployment insurance by working. But according to this section here, the fact that she got married immediately constitutes a separation from her employer. I do not think that is intended; but that is exactly how it can be interpreted and is how it is in fact being interpreted in a great many cases. As I said before, I think we might leave the suggested changes to the regulations with regard to married women, for further study on the part of all of us; and I will promise to bring the matter up again under the unemployment insurance item. This has been a week of conferences. It is true that the commission has also been meeting representatives of the hospital associations of Canada. I have here a brief statement. I know that a number of members have had telegrams, and that some hospitals have been worrying for fear that there was an attempt on the part of the commission to put the main part of the hospital staff under the regulations.
The unemployment insurance commission had a meeting on May 16 with representatives of hospital associations, other charitable organizations and the principal labour organizations to receive their views on its proposals for extending unemployment insurance coverage to some classes of employees in hospitals and charitable institutions.
The proposals made a year ago had been modified and it was suggested that only the administrative and maintenance workers be insured. Most of the persons in these groups were in occupations where they are normally insured when in industry. The commission did not propose to insure medical, nursing or technical staff. Clergymen and members of religious orders would of course remain noninsurable also.
Briefs were received from thirty-eight organizations and individuals. Fourteen supported the proposal. Twenty-four were opposed.
The hospital associations stated that they were in favour of unemployment insurance but could not support the proposal at present because of the additional cost. They saw no way of meeting this except by passing it on to the patients or curtailing their services.
The labour organizations felt that as most workers in hospitals and charitable institutions were in the lower paid groups, and as the turnover was fairly high, it was important that those in occupations where they would normally be insured elsewhere should not suffer an interruption of insurance when employed in similar occupations in hospitals and charitable institutions. They were therefore anxious to see at least the non-professional and general labour groups insured.
Supply-Labour
I might add here, those in small or medium-size hospitals are not very many, elevator people perhaps, some people on the office staff, carpenters and so forth.
The commission stated that it would give consideration to these representations before any action was taken. It might be possible to make further modifications in its proposals so as to provide insurance for the most vulnerable groups without making too serious an increase in costs.
I can assure hon. members that no drastic action is being taken. The matter is being explored very carefully in the light of all the representations that have been received.

the elevator workers, the charwomen and dishwashers, and such people as those, have a right to protection other than for charity's sake.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO ENACTMENT OF LEGISLATION AND APPROVAL OF UNITED NATIONS DECLARATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 14 the hon.
member for Rosetown-Biggar asked the following question, as reported at page 2980 of Hansard:
Will the government comply with the recent request . . . for the introduction in both houses of parliament this session of a resolution approving the inclusion in the Canadian constitution of a declaration of human rights and liberties, and that pending appropriate legislation such approval should affirm parliament's acceptance on behalf of Canada of the United Nations declaration of human rights?
The question asked by the hon. member divides itself into two parts.
The first part refers to the inclusion in the Canadian constitution of a declaration of human rights and liberties. This would require an amendment of the constitution affecting both the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures.
Under the present procedure such an amendment would have to be made by the parliament at Westminster, and this government would not recommend an application for such action by the parliament at Westminster without the consent of the provincial legislatures or governments.
The federal government is now discussing with the provincial governments the establishment of a satisfactory procedure to have future amendments to the constitution made by Canadian authorities here in Canada, and while these discussions are proceeding this government does not intend to initiate discussions about a matter like that referred to in the question, which is apt to be quite controversial and might retard the solution of the question relating to the establishment of a satisfactory procedure to make future amendments here in Canada.
As for the second part, the Canadian government has already, through the affirmative vote of the Canadian delegation in the general assembly of the United Nations, accepted the universal declaration of human rights as a general statement of principles to which we subscribe. Before the vote was taken on the declaration, the Canadian delegation stated that it had various reservations 80709-205J
on details of the text. The head of the Canadian delegation added that certain important aspects of the declaration were within the field of provincial jurisdiction, and that in regard to any rights defined in the document the federal government did not intend to invade that field of provincial jurisdiction.
Now, since this universal declaration of human rights is not a legal instrument, the government does not propose to ask parliament, in advance of the submission for signature of the proposed convention on the same subject which is now under consideration by the United Nations, to endorse the approval expressed by Canada through its delegation.

speechtext: Has the Department of National Health and Welfare taken any measures with respect to influenza in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
A national influenza centre has been established at the laboratory of hygiene with an advisory committee composed of a number of experts in virus diseases.
This centre is working in close co-operation with the world influenza centre in London, England, with the virus research centre at the Connaught Medical Research Laboratories at Toronto, and the regional centres in the United States, and exchanges with them the latest information on current epidemics and the development of new vaccines.
During the recent epidemic, our national influenza centre, in collaboration with the departments of health of all provinces, isolated and identified the influenza virus causing the epidemic. Comparative studies of this strain of virus revealed that it was identical with the strain which caused the recent epidemic in England.
In close co-operation with the American advisory committee on influenza, the problem of the efficacy of influenza vaccines was carefully studied in selected groups during the recent epidemic. These studies indicated that the older vaccines which were commercially available had little protective effect in this particular outbreak and newer improved vaccines are now being developed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (for ihe Minister of Labour) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: APPROVAL OF ILO CONVENTION FIXING MINIMUM AGE FOR EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA
speechtext: That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve of convention No. 58, fixing the minimum age for the admission of children to employment at sea (revised 1936) adopted by the general conference of the international labour organization at its 22nd session at Geneva on the 24th day of October, 1936, as modified by the final articles revision convention, 1946, and that this house do approve of the same.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. Cote (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: APPROVAL OF ILO CONVENTION FIXING MINIMUM AGE FOR EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this resolution is to obtain approval by parliament of a convention passed by the general conference of the international labour organization at Geneva at its 22nd session, October 24, 1936. Upon approval of its terms by parliament the government proposes to proceed to the ratification of the convention.
Convention No. 58 provides that children under the age of fifteen years shall not be employed for work on vessels other than vessels upon which only members of the same family are employed. There are two exceptions in the convention to this general provision. First, national laws may provide for the issue, in respect of children not less than fourteen years, of certificates permitting them
Labour Conditions
to be employed in cases in which an educational or other appropriate authority is satisfied, having due regard to the health and physical condition of the child and to the prospective as well as the immediate benefit to the child of the employment proposed, that such employment will be beneficial to the child. Second, the provision does not apply to work done by children on school ships or training ships, provided that such work is approved and supervised by public authority.
This parliament has already approved the principle contained in this convention, and has given effect to it by an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act contained in chapter 35 of the statutes of Canada, 1948, repealing the former section 279 of the said act, and substituting therefor a new section 279 which provides that no person under fifteen years of age shall be employed on any vessel, subject to specified exceptions which correspond to the exceptions contained in convention 58, which I have outlined above.
It will be evident that Canada is already in full compliance with the provisions of this convention, and that no new legislation is required for this purpose. The convention has been ratified by ten other countries, namely, Belgium, Brazil, Bulgaria, France, Iraq, The Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, and the United States. Canada ratified; an earlier ILO convention No. 7, in March, 1926, fixing the minimum age for admission of children to employment at sea at fourteen years of age. This convention is in fact a revision of convention No. 7.
Perhaps I should explain just what obligations follow upon the ratification of an ILO convention by a member state of the ILO. When the ratification has been communicated to the director of the international labour organization, the ratifying state is required to take such action as may then be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the convention by the enactment of legislation or otherwise if this has not already been done. Each of the member states ratifying the convention agrees to make periodic reports to the international labour office on the measures which it has taken to give effect to the provisions of the convention.
In effect, therefore, a member state ratifying a convention assumes the obligation that the provisions of the convention shall be given continuing effect, in that its legislation and practice on the subject matter of the convention provide labour standards on a level at least as high as the standards established by the provisions of the particular convention.

Labour Conditions
I therefore recommend to the house the adoption of this resolution.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. F. Higgins (St. John's East):
subtopic: APPROVAL OF ILO CONVENTION FIXING MINIMUM AGE FOR EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to delay the house at all on this matter. I imagine that will be welcome news. I have listened to the parliamentary assistant, and I have had the opportunity of studying the proposed resolution. It certainly appears to be one which should have the full commendation of the house. I understand that the principle has been endorsed already by some ten or eleven nations. It was adopted in 1936, and modified by the final articles revision convention in 1946. As all members are aware the ILO is now one of the specialized agencies of the United Nations, and I feel that as such any recommendation of this kind will have the general support of this house. I am sure that no hon. member wants to have children exploited as they have been in the past, and any measure to prohibit such exploitation is bound to have the approval of all hon. members.
There is one question which occurs to me, but I am sure there is a good explanation for it. I understand that the provision under family allowances is that the children must attend school until they are sixteen years of age, otherwise family allowances are not forthcoming. I presume the obvious explanation is that if children are working before they are sixteen-this measure provides that they may work after fifteen- there will be no need for family allowances. I suggest that is the only question about which there may be any doubt. Other than that, I see no reason why passage of this particular resolution should be delayed, and it should receive the wholehearted support of the house.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF ILO CONVENTION FIXING MINIMUM AGE FOR EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all members of the house will welcome the ratification, not only of this convention but of any other ILO convention, because the purpose is to improve the conditions of those who make their living by working for someone else. I believe this convention came into effect first in 1939, after it received* ratification by two members of the ILO. At this distance I could not hear everything the parliamentary assistant said*, but I was wondering why the 1936 convention was not ratified by this parliament. I am just wondering why ratification has been delayed until this late date.
The parliamentary assistant said that the terms of the convention are perhaps not as good as the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act. While that may be true, I think most of us have had sufficient experience with conventions of this kind to realize that

the terms of the convention do not mean very much. Unless there is adequate inspection to ensure that the convention is carried out, it may be only so many words on paper. I should like to have heard the parliamentary assistant explain the inspection provisions under the Canada Shipping Act which make sure that persons under fifteen years of age are not employed on any vessel except in conformity with the exceptions made in the convention. In this regard I would draw the attention of the house to a press release issued by the Department of Labour on February 8, 1951. The release was received from the ILO in Geneva, and concerns the health and welfare conditions of seamen who travel from port to port in various parts of the world. Their health conditions, the release pointed out, are such as to be a threat to the maritime nations as well as to the seamen themselves.
There are several conventions-I do not know whether we have ratified all of them -dealing with conditions on board ship and the health of seamen. Evidently they have been ratified by other maritime nations, and perhaps by our own. According to the press release I referred to, the enforcement of these conventions still leaves a great deal to be desired. I believe that this resolution should have been moved at a time when the house could go into committee, so that we could obtain information from the Minister of Labour and his experts as to how these conventions are carried out.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF ILO CONVENTION FIXING MINIMUM AGE FOR EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant whether in article 2, clause 1, which prohibits children under the age of fifteen from being employed, on vessels other than vessels upon which only members of the same family are employed, there is a loophole whereby children may be taken from school to work with their own family when they are under the age of fifteen. It is not very clear. Probably our own law is more explicit in that regard. I should like to know whether or not that is the case.
In clause 2 of the same article, reference is made to "national laws or regulations," and in the fifth line it reads: "appropriate authority designated by such laws or regulations is satisfied." Does that refer to national laws, or to the fact that provincial and local authorities have the sanction of national authority to issue these certificates?-as has been the case, of course, in Ontario with respect to children leaving school for employment other than on vessels.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF ILO CONVENTION FIXING MINIMUM AGE FOR EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of arguing

the merits or demerits of the resolution, but I should like to point out to the parliamentary assistant that this is a resolution which definitely should go before the committee on industrial relations. There is no hurry about this convention decision. It has been standing since 1936.
From listening to the parliamentary assistant I gained the impression that there is a reservation implied in this resolution as to the decision of the conference to exclude from the age limit laid down by the convention children employed on vessels on which only children of the same family are employed. I do not agree with that. I think it conflicts with the general principle of the resolution. In other words, the father, if he is so minded, can put the children, at ten years of age, aboard a vessel and thus exploit the family, ignoring much of the legislation that we have today with regard to what the province considers to be a proper educational standard before employment is permitted.
Some of the provinces have already established, for work purposes, a definite age limit. This convention decision is cutting right across provincial legislation, and I do not like the reservation that permits the father to exploit the family. The implications of this convention decision are sufficiently serious to justify reference of the resolution to the committee on industrial relations, so that we may at least gain a thorough understanding of what we are doing in accepting the proposal that is now before the house. I therefore move:
That this resolution and the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee cn industrial relations for investigation and report.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: APPROVAL OF ILO CONVENTION FIXING MINIMUM AGE FOR EMPLOYMENT OF CHILDREN AT SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the apprehensions of the hon. member who spoke last (Mr. Gillis) are not well founded. This exception in the convention would not override any legislation, whether federal or provincial. All that we undertake is that we will not have anything less stringent than what the convention provides. There are provincial regulations with respect to the obligation of parents to have their children attend school, and the exception contained in the convention would not override those regulations but would merely make it an obligation upon us, in the exercise of such jurisdiction as we may have, to endeavour to have the convention complied with. These international labour organization conventions require us to do everything within our jurisdiction that is necessary to compliance with them, and to use our best endeavours to get the other authorities who may have jurisdiction on any subject matter also to comply. But
Labour Conditions
the purpose of these conventions is merely to establish a minimum which the signatories are obliged to comply with; there is no implication that they cannot do more if they feel that more is better suited to the situation of their own country.
I do not think there can be any serious objection to having the resolution go before the industrial relations committee, if hon. members generally feel that they would like to discuss it there with the Minister of Labour or the officials of his department. By our own legislation we do more than is required by this convention; and the purpose of the ratification, as was suggested on another matter by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), is to assist the officials of the international labour organization to get an agreement from others who may not be doing as much as we are doing. If there is any desire to have the matter considered in the committee on industrial relations, the government would have no objection to that being done. I do not know that it is necessary; but if the hon. member insists on his amendment, the government will offer no objection.

Mr. Speaker, may I just make one or two observations in connection with this proposal? As to a number of these conventions which arise out of the deliberations of the special agencies of the United Nations and of international organizations, it seems to me that a procedure such as that which has been recommended by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) ought to be followed. When the conventions come before parliament, they come in the form of a resolution, and there is no opportunity in committee of the whole to interrogate anyone in the government; they sometimes also come in fairly detailed form, as does this convention. On previous occasions, when resolutions of a detailed nature of this kind have been before the house, I have felt that proper provision is not made under the rules for a proper and full discussion unless the matter goes before a special committee of the house.
When the parliamentary assistant rises to answer the questions that have been put to him during this short debate, perhaps he might indicate why we have delayed so long, a circumstance which was mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). If it was a good convention-and I agree that it is-surely it should have been

approved long ago. Delaying action of this kind only indicates that this parliament may have had some doubt as to the principle of it, and I think that any such doubt should have been removed long before now.
In addition we ought to know from the parliamentary assistant the dates upon which these various nations officially ratified the convention. That would indicate how far we are behind, or whether we are only keeping abreast of some other slow people in other parts of the world.
