speechtext:
I had assumed that would be what hon. members would wish; and the statement I have to make is purely supplementary to the statements made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself a week or two ago.
Hon. members will recall that when the results of the Torquay tariff conference were announced in the house some two weeks ago, my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a comprehensive statement outlining the benefits which Canada will receive under the new trade agreements. At that time I also spoke on the changes in the Canadian customs tariff which we had agreed to make as part of the Torquay agreements. In addition my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) issued a fairly lengthy press release outlining in somewhat greater detail the results of the conference. It is therefore unnecessary to cover that ground again today, but I would like to supplement the previous statements with a few explanatory remarks.
When the Prime Minister presented the resolution referring the Torquay agreements to the standing committee on banking and commerce, he referred to a number of documents which embody the results of the Torquay negotiations. These documents are somewhat technical and complicated. A brief explanation of what they contain may be helpful to the house in its consideration of the resolution.
First, a word about the final act of Torquay. This is a purely formal document, authenticating texts of the legal instruments which were drawn up to give effect to the agreements reached at Torquay. It simply states that representatives of the signatory countries had assembled at Torquay for the purpose of carrying out tariff negotiations; that they had achieved
Trade Agreements
certain results; and that the results described in the accompanying instruments do in fact describe accurately what had been done. The final act was signed at the close of the conference by all the participating governments. All the other legal instruments which the Prime Minister mentioned in the resolution are annexed to the Torquay final act.
Annex I to the final act contains the decisions agreeing to the accession of six new countries to the general agreement on tariffs and trade. From the very inception of the general agreement in 1947 provision was made to allow additional countries to join the agreement and so enjoy its benefits, provided, of course, that they enter into negotiations with a view to granting tariff concessions equivalent in value to the concessions made by the original members. The question of admitting new countries is of vital concern to all members because, as hon. members know, under the most-favourednation clause once a country is accepted into the agreement it is automatically entitled to all the tariff concessions granted in the course of the three sets of tariff negotiations held under the general agreement since 1947. Hon. members will recall that these three sets of negotiations occurred as follows: 23 countries at Geneva in 1947, 33 countries at Annecy in 1949, and 34 countries at Torquay in 1951. In order to ensure that the new countries do in fact make adequate payment for membership, the agreement provides that a two-thirds majority of the present membership is needed before a decision can be taken to admit a new country. In this way, by giving members an opportunity to pass judgment on the value of the tariff concessions offered by the countries seeking admission to the group, the principle of reciprocity and mutual advantage is protected.
One of the main purposes of the Torquay conference was to increase the over-all value of the general agreement by expanding it to include Austria, the German federal republic, Korea, Peru, the Philippines and Turkey. As hon. members know, Canada concluded successful agreements with all those countries. Accordingly, together with the United Kingdom, United States, and other important countries, we are prepared to indicate readiness to accept them into the general agreement by signing the decisions agreeing to their accession. The last day for signing these decisions is June 20. It is expected that the necessary two-thirds majority will be forthcoming on behalf of all the new countries, so that they will all become members shortly after that

Trade Agreements
date. Canada will extend the benefits of its tariff concessions to the new countries after they have been formally accepted, as members and have extended their tariff concessions to Canada.
Annex II to the final act contains the Torquay protocol to the general agreement on tariffs and trade. The Torquay protocol is the principal instrument which emerged from the conference and, I believe, the document in which hon. members will be mainly interested. It is designed to achieve three things. First, it contains the detailed terms and procedures under which the new countries will be admitted to the agreement. Second, it amends the general agreement in order to extend the Geneva and Annecy tariff concessions for a further period of three years. Third, it embodies the results of all the tariff negotiations undertaken at Torquay. These results are contained in a series of tariff schedules annexed to the protocol, one for each of the present members, and one for each of the acceding countries.
I do not intend to review in detail the legal terms of accession which make up the bulk of the protocol, because they are quite technical and not of general interest. Briefly, the terms of accession provide for reciprocal rights and obligations, so that new countries will be essentially in the same position as the present members. I would, however, like to say a wordi about the arrangement to extend the Geneva and Annecy concessions for a further period of three years, because this is one of the important achievements of the Torquay conference. As hon. members know, one of the main purposes of the general agreement is to reduce tariffs and other trade barriers to reasonable levels, and in this way to stabilize the conditions of world commerce by agreement among the principal trading nations not to raise their customs duties beyond certain agreed maximum rates. Prior to the general agreement there were, of course, many bilateral agreements in which countries undertook not to raise tariffs on specified items for certain fixed periods of time. While these agreements did provide an element of stability in tariff levels between nations, they did not go far enough, because there were large areas of trade not covered by such agreements. The general agreement drawn up in 1947 was an attempt to overcome this element of instability in world tariff levels. This agreement, which includes all the principal trading nations, together accounting for over 80 per cent of world trade, was a most significant achievement in the field of international co-operation since the end of the war.
The reductions and bindings in the rates of customs duties which were negotiated at

Geneva in 1947 and at Annecy in 1949 had an assured life only to January 1, 1951. Beyond that date the tariff concessions would remain in force, subject, however, to the right of members to make modifications or withdrawals after giving appropriate notice. It was felt that if the Geneva and Annecy concessions became liable to widespread modification or withdrawal, the stability of world tariff levels, one of the main benefits afforded by the agreement, would be imperilled. It was also quite clear that before further progress could be made by way of a new scaling down of high tariff barriers, or before additional countries would agree to accept membership, a decision would have to be taken with respect to the status of the original tariff concessions. Accordingly Canada, together with the United Kingdom and the United States, proposed that the previous agreements be extended for a further firm period of three years. This proposal was accepted by all the participating countries, and with minor modifications the original concessions were extended until January 1, 1954. Agreement on this basic issue paved the way for a large number of new tariff concessions among existing members, as well as with the six new countries. The formal amendment, extending the agreements for a further three years, will come into effect when the Torquay protocol has been signed by two-thirds of the present members. In the meantime, however, in order to secure the position until the formal amendment comes into force, the participating countries signed a declaration undertaking not to exercise their right to modify or withdraw tariff concessions prior to January 1, 1954. This declaration is contained in annex III to the final act.
Finally, I should like to say a word about the tariff schedules which are annexed to the Torquay protocol. These schedules, one for each of the participating governments, contain all the tariff items on which countries undertook not to raise their customs duties beyond the maximum rates stated therein for a period of three years. In most cases the rates shown in these schedules are reductions from existing rates, while in other cases they represent bindings of present customs duties against increase. There are thirty-seven such schedules, and the one allocated to Canada is schedule V which, as members of the house will recall, I tabled on May 8. The Torquay tariff schedules supplement and, in some instances, modify similar schedules which emerged from the previous conferences held at Geneva and Annecy. In order to get a comprehensive picture of the whole range of tariff items now covered by the general agreement, one would have to look at the separate

tariff schedules which were drawn up at Geneva, at Annecy, and finally at Torquay. I understand that the secretariat is now in process of preparing consolidated tariff schedules showing, under one cover for each of the countries, all the tariff concessions granted under the general agreement on tariffs and trade since 1947.
The legal documentation embodying the results of the Torquay negotiations is, as you might expect, voluminous, so that we have only published the Canadian schedule V. I believe copies of schedule V have been distributed to all members of the house. The schedules of tariff concessions by all the countries, and the text of the Torquay protocol, have been published by the secretariat at Geneva and released in limited numbers on May 12. We are endeavouring to obtain sufficient copies, and these will be distributed to all members of the standing committee on banking and commerce as soon as they are available.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that after this resolution has been discussed and passed by the house, the question of this agreement can be fully considered by the banking and commerce committee where, as I indicated the other day, Mr. Hector McKinnon, chairman of the tariff board, who was one of our principal negotiators at Torquay, as well as other members, will be available to answer any questions hon. members may have in connection with the Torquay agreement, or the proceedings at Annecy and Geneva.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: MATTER TO BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I expect that there will be general approval of the decision of the government to refer the Torquay agreement to the banking and commerce committee as proposed in this resolution. My remarks are directed, first of all, to the general effect of the Torquay arrangements, and second as to the essential considerations which it seems to me should be before that committee in addition to the consideration of the Torquay agreement itself. While this resolution deals exclusively with the results of the Torquay agreements, and the documents related to those agreements, the banking and commerce committee will of course have full authority to make such other recommendations as may appear to be appropriate in the light of the Torquay arrangements.
It is with that thought in mind I wish to make some observations concerning the Torquay agreement, and also on the general subject of trade. We cannot regard the Torquay decisions in a vacuum, but must regard them as part of an integrated picture of our world trade as a whole. I am speaking in that respect of Canada, and of the impact
Trade Agreements
of those arrangements upon Canada at this time. First of all, I believe it is desirable that the Torquay agreement be kept in perspective, because, if there is a tendency to overemphasize the results of what took place there, there may be the same tendency to overlook other matters that are of equally great or perhaps greater importance, having regard to our long-range picture of world trade.
Undoubtedly the presentation of the results of that conference by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and the supplementary statement made public by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), did leave the impression that tremendous gains had been made at Torquay. I believe it will be necessary for all of us to wait and see exactly what happens before we assess in very precise terms exactly what the effeot of the Torquay agreement is going to be upon Canada or upon the other countries. But one of the things which it seems to me might well be in the minds of the members of the banking and commerce committee in considering these agreements, and any other recommendations that they think it desirable to make, is that the headlines in the press are not, in themselves, going to bring results. It would be unfortunate if, through the great headlines that were given to the Torquay agreement, we got the idea that these agreements alone were going to produce immense gains for Canada.
I believe all hon. members of this house will welcome whatever extension of trade has resulted, or will result in the future, from these agreements. But there are definite limitations upon the results that can flow from those agreements, which it would be a good thing to keep in mind when we are considering the whole problem of world trade. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated that at the moment we have no worries about marketing our products. Undoubtedly that statement interprets the unusual situation in which we find ourselves at the moment, with certain reservations. The fact is that already there does seem to be some concern as to whether there may not be too great exports of some particular products.
The first thing that all of us are naturally concerned about is the longer picture of the future, and what is going to happen in the years ahead. Unfortunately it would appear that, in so far as greatly broadening world trade is concerned, Torquay has not lived up to the expectations of those who went there from the different nations that attended that important conference. For one thing, there was the effective burial of the international

Trade Agreements
trade organization, to which so many people had attached such great hopes. It may well be that some other organization will emerge which will give alternative advantages. When we consider, however, the great expectations that were attached to the international trade organization, the demise of ITO cannot in itself be regarded with any considerable measure of satisfaction until we know what is going to take its place.
The London Economist, which is regarded as a modest and extremely well-informed publication in dealing with matters of this kind, put it in these words:
ITO itself disappeared, with all the hopes built upon it, into the limbo of stillborn international organizations.
This is a time when all of us are hoping to strengthen international organization and to extend in every way possible a wider and wider association in international trade and in other fields of international co-operation. For that reason it seems to me that the demise of ITO is a regrettable feature of the discussions at Torquay.
Generally, the financial observers of this country have been inclined to modify greatly the first glowing reports which were given of these agreements when they were announced. As an example, a recent discussion of this subject in the Montreal Financial Times of May 11 is headed "Torquay Tariff Agreements Show Meagre Results." In the Financial Post published in Toronto, giving its general impressions of Torquay, we find the heading: "Little Gained from Torquay". These headings merely indicate the moderation with which we should accept the glowing statements that were made about the agreements and about their advantage to Canada. In the Winnipeg Free Press, for instance-which is generally favourable to the point of view expressed by the government in matters of this kind-their discussion of Torquay is headed "Trade Liberalization Postponed." Another heading, this time in the Windsor Daily Star of April 21, describes tha general effect of the article under the heading as follows: "Wilgress Says Results Not So Great". Then in the body of a Reuters news agency dispatch from Torquay the conference chairman, L. Dana Wilgress of Canada, is said to have gloomily reported: "The results are not as great as many had hoped."
Mr. Speaker, these statements indicate reasons why this house should consider other aspects of world trade. Before this house discusses this subject again, the banking and commerce committee should be considering other aspects of world trade so that we shall not alone be dealing with the results of the Torquay conference at the time that

this matter comes back before us for further consideration. If we become victims of the illusions created by the headlines which accompanied the formal announcement in this house of the Torquay agreements, then we may be diverted from the attention that should be given to other problems of trade which are of as great importance as and, in some cases, perhaps of greater importance than, the Torquay negotiations and the agreements which resulted from them.
I think that the committee on banking and commerce, in recognizing that the Torquay agreements relate to only a segment of the whole problem of world trade for Canada, might well take into consideration the recommendation made by a meeting of representatives of industry and commerce in Great Britain and Canada when they met in Toronto on May 18. At that meeting, which took place only three days ago, leading manufacturers and businessmen from Britain and from Canada discussed various problems of world trade and the possibility of extending it. The recommendation to which that meeting attached the greatest importance, and the one which received the most attention in the public discussion at that conference in Toronto, was that steps should be taken immediately-and may I emphasize that word "immediately"-to convene a conference of the governments of the nations of the commonwealth and of the other countries of the empire, for the purpose of extending trade within the commonwealth and empire, and of finding a solution of those problems and difficulties which today are raising barriers against that trade.
This conference which was simply an informal meeting of high-ranking representatives of business and commerce in both Canada and Great Britain was attended by men of outstanding experience; and I would mention the fact that, in addition to the general recommendation that the possibility of expanding trade and commerce within the commonwealth and empire be explored, they also urged the consideration of the possibility of finding some solution for the problem of making the pound and the dollar convertible.
I would recall to your mind, Mr. Speaker, the fact that on February 28 of last year we placed before this house a resolution urging the convening of such a conference. At that time the government did not see fit to accede to the arguments we presented in support of such a conference. In fact the suggestion was made that such a conference could not be productive of useful results at that time.
Now we have a recommendation of the very highest ranking businessmen from

Canada and Great Britain, urging that there be a commonwealth economic conference at the earliest practical date. This, it seems to me, ties right in with the discussion of the Torquay agreements, because the value of the Torquay agreements, or otherwise, will depend very largely upon their relationship to trade within the commonwealth itself. Having said that, I would impress upon this house and, through the statements in this house, to members of the banking and commerce committee, that there is good reason for the sense of urgency behind that recommendation of the meeting in Toronto last week of the Anglo-Canadian trade committee.
I think this would be an appropriate time to recall what has happened to our export business to the United Kingdom. At the very time that our exports to the United States have been mounting so rapidly, our exports to the United Kingdom have been diminishing to a very dangerous extent. These are the figures from 1943 on, in millions of dollars, in exports to the United States: 1943, $1,149 million; 1944, $1,301 million; 1945, $1,197 million; 1946, $888 million; 1947, $1,034 million; 1948, $1,501 million; 1949, $1,503 million; 1950, $2,021 million. Placed side by side with the export figures to the United Kingdom, we see what has been happening in the percentage of exports going to our two greatest export markets. In 1943 our exports in dollars to the United Kingdom amounted to $1,033 million; 1944, $1,235 million; 1945, $963 million; 1946, $597 million; 1947, $751 million; 1948, $687 million; 1949, $705 million; 1950; $470 million. Thus, whereas in 1943 our exports to the United Kingdom and to the United' States were in reasonable balance, amounting as they did1 to $1,149 million to the United States and $1,033 million to the United Kingdom, we find that last year the export? to the United States were $2,021 million and to the United Kingdom only $470 million. That represents in dollar value a drop to 37 per cent of what our exports were to the United Kingdom in 1943; but that itself does not give the whole picture, because, if we take the basic dollar value used by the dominion bureau of statistics in its regular cost of living index, we find that our dollar in 1943 had a value of 84 cents; whereas last year, or early this year, it had a value of approximately 55 cents. Thus we find that the actual value of exports to the United Kingdom in terms of equalized dollars amounts to only something just less than 30 per cent of what it was in 1943.
One of the answers, and one of the very important answers, to this difficult situation
Trade Agreements
is the inconvertibility of the dollar, which has raised difficulties within the period I have mentioned. These businessmen; these financial, hardheaded, experienced men, who have been dealing in international trade and in international finance for many years, came to the conclusion at this gathering of the Anglo-Canadian trade committee that steps should be taken immediately to convene a conference of governments of the commonwealth at the earliest practical date to tackle this whole problem interpreted in those dollar figures that I have given, and to seek ways of breaking the log-jam that is threatening our traditional trade channels in the years ahead.
We have every reason to welcome the extension and expansion of trade with the United States. On many occasions in this house, long before any recent comments about the fact that Canada must not be a satellite of the United States, members of the party to which I belong have urged that we should make sure that we did not become a satellite of the United' States by making sure that we preserved an appropriate balance in our world trade so that no matter how friendly our relationships with the United States might be we would not have all our eggs in one basket, and not find ourselves economically dependent upon the United States although we do regard them with such friendship. It was with that very thought in mind that on more than one occasion during the past years this party has presented motions calling for an economic conference of the nations of the commonwealth to find ways to remove those barriers, to break this log-jam of dollar-pound inconvertibility, and generally to lay the trade basis for first of all the recovery of our commonwealth markets, and then the expansion of those markets in the years ahead.
By all means, let us seek the expansion of our trade with the United States; but let us remember that this country is set up for trading with the United Kingdom and the commonwealth. That was not done with any thought of placing barriers between the United States and Canada. Our ties of blood, our ties of friendship and our ties of history are too close for the effective erection of barriers between the peoples of the United States and Canada, who know each other better than the peoples of any other two nations in the whole world.
But that does not get away from the fact that this country has recognized from the earliest days that our production is largely parallel with and not complementary to that of the United States. One of the reasons we have been able to export such enormous

Trade Agreements
quantities to the United States has been one which none of us can welcome. Undoubtedly one of the reasons why there was such a tremendous increase last year in the dollar value of exports was the tremendous stockpiling that is taking place in the United States. Much of that business was abnormal; much of that business was business which took from Canada raw materials which, to the great advantage of our own people, we could be fabricating in Canada.
I suggest we should examine with great care many of the lines of raw materials and products we exported last year to the United States, and we should consider whether it is desirable that exports on that level, of those particular raw materials and commodities, should continue in future years. I do not wish to have that statement interpreted at any time as a suggestion that I do not welcome Canada's full participation in any joint steps which are necessary for the building up of the mutual strength of each of these nations. I suggest however that we should recognize why it was that the figure rose so rapidly from $1,503 million in 1949 which, up to that time was a record in dollar value of exports, to $2,021 million last year. The preparation for the defence of freedom was part of the reason for that great increase.
Along with that we see the alarming drop from the figure of $705 million in dollar value of exports to the United Kingdom in 1949-and this amount was less than half of the value of exports to the United States in that year-to the tragically and dangerously low figure of $470 million in 1950-and that figure is even lower than it appears, if we consider the depreciated value of the dollar. It will be noted that this last-mentioned figure is not much more than one-fifth of our value of exports to the United States.
There are many reasons why, by every device within our power, we should be seeking to find a solution for the problem of convertibility of the dollar and the pound as between Canada and the United Kingdom. That is our first problem. I think we should not be unwilling to explore the problem with the government of the United Kingdom and other governments throughout the commonwealth, without waiting for any general solution of the problem by the international organization built up under the United Nations.
After all, if for military purposes it is found satisfactory for a limited number of nations within the United Nations to deal with a particular military problem, as we have in respect of Korea, and as we did earlier in respect of the Atlantic nations, then I say that in the field of international trade there

is no reason whatever why nations of the commonwealth should not seek a solution of this problem, to their own advantage and to the advantage of every trading nation in the world.
If we can find a solution to this problem as between Canada and other nations in the commonwealth, we shall have found the key which will unlock the door to vast trading possibilities throughout the whole world, which are being held back by this one almost insuperable problem. Today we are nearer this possibility than we have been at any time since the dollar and the pound were declared inconvertible. The very fact that it was necessary for the United States to buy essential requirements last year in such large quantities throughout the whole world has eased the dollar problem to an extent it has not been eased since this major difficulty first arose in the post-war period. For that reason I do believe that, when dollars are flowing to nations for essential defence supplies, we should seize this opportunity to seek a solution of the problem.
In a speech delivered in London over a year ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated why he thought trading possibilities between our two countries should not be limited by any artificial barriers of this kind. His statement was welcomed then by the United Kingdom, and I believe found general approval at that time. He was pointing out that, at a time when there are hungry nations in the world, it seems illogical that we should sit back and do nothing to break down the barriers which are preventing our selling food supplies we can produce in such quantities and which the people of other nations need so badly.
We can produce a great deal more. We can produce a great deal more of many types of essential products. It has been said over and over again that ohe of the devices by which we can most effectively fight communism is to see that there is ample food throughout the world. Today India, a sister nation in the commonwealth, is in many sections facing real and terrible starvation. Without delay, not only as a practical gesture of health and friendship, but also as evidence of our partnership within the commonwealth, Canada should make available to India all the wheat we can possibly spare to ship at this critical time.
Quite apart from that, we should be finding ways in which nations within the commonwealth which need our food supplies can buy that food, and buy it very largely through the rotating exchange which would be possible if we were able to break down this

barrier of inconvertibility. There are humanitarian reasons; there are business reasons. There are reasons related to the strength of the British partnership itself which all suggest that when the Torquay agreements are before the committee on banking and commerce that committee should also consider this recommendation, which has been made in such urgent terms by the Anglo-Canadian trade committee.
I hope that when the banking and commerce committee reports to the house it will report not only on the Torquay agreements but also on other aspects of related trade, and that it will recommend that without any delay whatever the Canadian government, which is in a unique position to take such action, being the one nation of the commonwealth which deals in dollars rather than in pounds, should take the necessary steps to bring together a conference of the nations of the commonwealth to seek every possible means of extending trade and removing any barriers which still hinder the extension of trade and of contact of every kind within this great fellowship.

subsubtopic: MATTER TO BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that all of us who followed the Torquay conferences hoped that the name of Torquay might be associated with a much wider reduction of tariffs than was there achieved. I quite agree with what has already been said that, as far as one is able to see from the schedules that have been published in some of the newspapers, there is very little indeed that gives any hope of a really wide extension of trade and commerce. In his last few words I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) indicated that he had overlooked the content of the resolution. The wording of the resolution is as follows:
That the subject matter of the Torquay negotiations, namely, the final act of Torquay; the decisions agreeing to accession; the Torquay protocol to the general agreement on tariffs and trade; the modifications of the schedules to the general agreement on tariffs and trade resulting from the Torquay negotiations . . .
And so on. The committee is not ordered to report back to the house. In December, 1947, there was a resolution on the order paper dealing with the Geneva agreements. It died on the order paper although we had been brought here specifically to discuss the Geneva agreements. The present resolution merely refers the subject matter of what took place at Torquay, and the results that were obtained, to the banking and commerce committee. They are not asked to report or to recommend anything.
Indeed the government has the right to make certain reductions or modifications in
Trade Agreements
our tariff schedules by order in council. In other words, we are not requested as a parliament to confirm anything that the government might do with respect to reduction of tariffs under agreements of this description. Neither at Geneva, at Annecy nor at Torquay were changes made in our tariff schedules that required the approval of parliament. I imagine that the resolution is in this form because of the authority that the government now has. What we are really doing under the resolution is merely referring the subject matter to the banking and commerce committee in order that that committee may call before it the officials responsible for these negotiations and for arriving at the conclusions reached at Torquay.
In passing may I say that I think the committee of representatives we had at Torquay, headed by Mr. Hector McKinnon, was an exceedingly able one, and I am sure they did their level best to safeguard the interests of Canada. However, as far as we are concerned this afternoon, let me repeat that all we are doing is referring the subject matter of these agreements and conclusions reached to the banking and commerce committee for their study. All they need do at the end of their study is to do what was done with the Geneva agreements, transmit the evidence and report to the house that the committee has studied and considered the matter referred to them. No recommendations will be required of the committee. Indeed under a resolution of this kind no recommendations could be made to the house that would be at all helpful to us or enable us to modify these agreements in any way.
Like the leader of the opposition-and I am sure in this respect all parties in the house agree-we regret that the international trade organization has failed to do what we hoped it would under the United Nations. I do not think there are any members who do not realize that the freeing of the channels of international trade is one of the great problems confronting the world. Indeed the need to free those channels and, as the leader of the opposition indicated, at the same time have a universal currency in which all our values could be expressed and to which our trade relationships could be related, makes it clear that convertibility of the dollar and the pound is of great interest not only to the world but particularly to the country in which we live.
Our whole economy was built up in the past on what has sometimes been referred to as the Atlantic triangle. We sold vast quantities of goods to Great Britain and the sterling area generally, and with the credits we obtained from our trade with that area

Trade Agreements
we were able to purchase vast quantities of goods from the United States. I am one of those who believe that at the present time our trading relationships are not healthy. While it has been valuable to increase our exports to the United States in the spectacular manner that we have, I believe that in reality that is not a sign of health so far as our economy is concerned. At the same time, as has already been pointed out, we have seen our exports to the United Kingdom drop proportionately. When we consider what our exports are from Canada to the United, States we realize that they are largely made necessary because of the international situation and also because of the depletion of United States resources. The wasteful manner in which the forests and the great iron ore deposits have been exploited has compelled the United States to look across the border, with considerable interest and some envy, at the great resources of this country. Our exports to the United States perhaps are not the sign of a healthy economy we would like to think they are. We may find,-perhaps not within the next few years, because the international situation may prevent it-that if and when the United States again builds up surpluses of goods, as she did in the past, she will no longer want many of the products and commodities we are now exporting to her, because she will no longer need them. Those of us who have lived in western Canada for any number of years have seen occasions when the United States was willing to take all the cattle and other commodities we could send her; but the time came when the United States was not able or willing to absorb the exports we had been sending, and we found ourselves cut off from the market we had built up. Of course to some extent that also applies to other markets, but in many instances and many respects I think the United States has been our most uncertain market.
As has been said already this afternoon, in many respects our economy, and particularly our agricultural economy, is not complementary to that of the United States, as it is to that of Great Britain and the sterling area. It is distinctly competitive. When surpluses occur in the United States, under the peculiar congressional system in that country powerful blocs can exert sufficient pressure upon members of congress and congress itself so that we may find ourselves in a very embarrassing position. I quite agree that we should do everything we can to encourage the maintenance and expansion of our trade with the United Kingdom and the sterling area, but I do not think we should go back to 1932 and in the building up of our
[Mr. Coldwell.l
trade with the commonwealth do anything that would be restrictive. If we entered into trading negotiations and arrived at trade agreements that were restrictive, in the sense that we were building trade within the commonwealth-if that were possible today, which I do not believe it is-we would be interfering with that larger expansion of trade at which I think we must all aim.
This agreement, like the others, is largely a matter of reciprocity in the hope that the nations agreeing at Torquay may obtain mutual advantages; and after all it is on mutual advantage that trading relationships are built. I hope we shall obtain more from this agreement than appears likely at the moment. Like most hon. members, I am sure, I have been able only to look over these schedules and get some general impressions of them. I do not note that the concessions we are making to other countries, particularly in regard to commodities we get from the United States, are offset to the extent some of us had hoped by the concessions we are getting from the United States and other countries. However, that is a first impression, which may be dissipated when the banking and commerce committee is able to question the representatives who negotiated this agreement on behalf of Canada. As things stand in the world today I think one of the satisfactory features of the negotiations is that the Geneva and Annecy agreements have been extended until January 1, 1954. At least that gives some guarantee of stabilization during that period and removes some uncertainty in our trading relationships. The reductions that are made are to come into effect, so the minister told us a few minutes ago, on June 20; but only, I believe, if they come into effect on that date mutually. We are not obligated to put anything into effect until the country with which we have negotiated is prepared to put into effect the mutual concession. I think the object of the extension of the agreements for three years, to prevent increases in these tariffs during that time, is something we should all welcome in this house; but really what I rose to say was that while we support this resolution referring to the committee the subject matter of these negotiations and agreements, we think it would have been well if we could have had a report and some recommendations from that committee so that we could have discussed the wider issues involved under these Torquay arrangements.
I do not intend to say more. I believe one of my colleagues is going to deal with several specific matters connected with these agreements. I do hope, however, that the agreements whir l have been made-Geneva,

Annecy, Torquay-will never be regarded either by the government or by anyone else as a substitute for what we hoped might be done under the international trade organization of the United Nations. It seems to me that if we are going to build up the kind of world we hope to see we must have a freer flow of commodities all across the world, and that free flow must be in the nature of a two-way traffic. We cannot expect to sell in markets where we do not buy. Then, as was said a few moments ago, we must also consider the effect on the improvement in standards of living, so that Canada may play her part in meeting the threat to the world caused by the poverty, misery, want and economic insecurity to be found over such a large portion of the globe at the present time.

subsubtopic: MATTER TO BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is a matter of regret to us, Mr. Speaker, that' this resolution in the name of the Prime Minister does not provide for a report and recommendations to be made to this house after the committee has studied the Torquay agreements and decisions. I feel, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has just expressed himself, that much good may be lost in this discussion since no provision has been made for a report and recommendations by the committee.
We are keenly interested, Mr. Speaker, in any proposals for the expansion of world trade on a basis mutually satisfactory to all countries concerned. Possibly we may find in the subject matter of the Torquay negotiations, that is the final act of Torquay and the decisions agreeing to the annexations and so on named in this resolution, some evidence that the barriers to satisfactory trading relations between nations have been removed to a certain extent. I hope so. I am not fully enough acquainted with what happened at Torquay to be able to assess that, but I look forward to the study in the banking and commerce committee, and perhaps we shall have something to say at the conclusion of the studies there. I am hoping that the real debate will take place when the committee reports to the house, because then we shall have much more information on which to base a sound judgment.
We do welcome, however, any agreements that lead to the removal of barriers, and to a mutually satisfactory type of trading relations. Over the years in this house I believe we have made our position quite clear, that is that we were working towards a type of trading relationship which would result in a balance, not necessarily a balance between two countries, but a balance between any one country and the rest of the world. We are still convinced, Mr. Speaker, that this
Trade Agreements
ideal, towards which we are labouring constantly, can only be reached if the great trading nations of the world will determine now, or at any rate soon, to buy from the rest of the world as much as they wish to sell to the rest of the world. Only by so doing can the currency with which to trade be made available.
We have been trying to follow an almost impossible method of trade. This matter of the convertibility of currencies, which has been one of the principles laid down upon which satisfactory trading relations can be carried on, is a fool's dream under present circumstances. There can only be convertibility of currencies if the great trading nations like United States, Canada, and Great Britain are prepared to purchase from the rest of the world goods to an amount equal to those which they are prepared to sell to the world. Now, I am afraid that Torquay has not made too many strides towards that ideal. It does not appear that is so, although we shall reserve a decision on that matter until such time as we have had a chance to examine more carefully what did come out of Torquay.
We welcome, Mr. Speaker, whatever reduced tariffs have been effected, particularly any movement towards a reduction to a reasonable level of tariff barriers. Now, that does not mean to say that we favour absolutely free trade, because we try to be realistic about it. Under present circumstances, no country could possibly remove all its tariffs. No country could go on a completely free trade basis. We must reserve the right to preserve our economic defences, and tariffs certainly constitute one of the bases of economic defence. I am afraid that we went a bit far in that regard under the Bretton Woods agreement. I am afraid we did agree there to surrender too many of our defences; tariff reductions or increases were amongst those that we did surrender. We have been breaking that agreement right and left ever since it was made. We have been ignoring it in many respects, indicating how foolish it was to enter into it in the first place.
In any event, we welcome whatever Torquay did to reduce tariffs to a reasonable level, so that there will be as few barriers to trade as possible. We are going to carefully study exactly what they were. We like the idea, which we have been constantly advocating, of a commonwealth economic conference. We feel that the commonwealth should and could be a great balancing factor in a world of trade unbalance. I do not know of any better way to try to restore balance, in a world of unbalance of trade, than to promote

Trade Agreements
the solidarity of the commonwealth and agreement amongst ourselves-not restrictive agreement, but at any rate a solidarity that would be in many respects comparable to our good neighbour to the south of us in its industrial capacity first, and in its trading possibilities second. It would only be through having such a solid commonwealth bloc that we could possibly impress upon nations like the United States the importance of attempting to balance trade. I do not see any other way. Certainly, there is much merit in what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has suggested in that regard.
We are interested not only in those things, Mr. Speaker; we are also especially interested in what progress might have been made at Torquay in connection with the principle of discrimination. One could speak at great length about that matter, but inasmuch as we are in the dark concerning what was accomplished at Torquay with respect to discrimination, we have to reserve anything we might want to say about it until after we have had our study in the committee. But let me say this. If the world is still crippled through having to accept the unconditional mostfavoured-nation clause in all trading agreements, then I am afraid Torquay has not accomplished very much. I am interested in finding out particularly just how far the foolish discriminations that are involved in the so-called unconditional most-favourednation clause have been removed. We have suffered, and other nations of the commonwealth have suffered, as a result of that foolish clause. We have fought wars over it, and I am afraid that unless the clause is modified, or unless it is thrown out altogether sometime and a much broader, more humanitarian principle imposed in its place, it will cause many more wars. I am going to reserve further discussion on that matter until I see just what the investigation in the committee brings out.
I am interested, and all of our group here are, Mr. Speaker, in what is going to be the future market for Canadian wheat and farm products. When I express that interest I have in mind what happened in 1949 and 1950, almost a godsend to the Canadian people, when the United States was prepared to spend over $960 million for Canadian farm products to send over to Europe under the ECA program. If it had not been for that, I just wonder where we would have found a market for that wheat and those farm products.

I read from the London Times:
As a result of seven months of negotiations at Torquay (which are the subject of a white paper issued yesterday) the general agreement on tariffs and trade is to remain in force for another three years. This means that the reductions of import duties and the other measures to remove restrictive practices in international trade which were agreed upon at Geneva and Annecy are now renewed until 1954. This was no foregone conclusion. By the beginning of 1950 many European countries were restoring their protective duties to at least the prewar level. There was growing-and, in the end, successful-opposition in America to the Havana charter for an international trade organization. It is a matter for some congratulation that the effort to bring about freer world trade is to be continued after all.
So that they gleaned some comfort-perhaps not a great deal-out of the results. Then they go on to point out that there are some gains. I read again from the London Times:
The Torquay negotiations have achieved some new reductions in customs duties, and some new countries-above all, western Germany-have been brought into the general agreement.
Then they make a comment which I think is an extremely shrewd one. They say that probably one of the reasons that even a modicum of success was achieved was this, and I think this is a shrewd comment:
Probably the return of the sellers' market since the spring of last year is largely responsible; it has again dulled the edge of competition, and for the time being, fewer manufacturers feel the need for protection.
I suppose there is a certain amount of truth in that, and it raises in one's mind the question whether the period of active trade and of seller's market is not one which if at all possible should be availed of for the purpose of doing away with more restrictions.
Then they go on to speak about the imperial preference, and they have one or two things to say about that which I think are important. They had one very interesting comment, namely, the difference in attitude of the United States as between imperial preference and the Sohuman agreement. I was interested in that partly because I was at Strasbourg last summer when they were discussing the Schuman agreement. I will read again from the Times because I think they put it very well. They say:
Any failure in commercial negotiations with America is to be regretted. It had been hoped 1bat some valuable concessions which would have aided the increase of sterling sales in the chief dollar market might have been obtained. The Americans asked for concessions in return which the British government were not prepared to make, and they were above all anxious for a further reduction of imperial preferences. They wished to make arrangements with the members of the commonwealth one by one, for reducing the preferences which they give, without consulting the other member countries who benefit from them. This

approach was rejected. With some reservations, all the proposed reductions of imperial preferences have been discussed by all the commonwealth countries concerned and in the end very few concessions have been made. The chief changes have come out of negotiations between Canada and the United States; they are a token of the strong natural attraction of trade over the Canadian frontier-and possibly also of Canadian disappointment over the restricted market afforded for Canadian goods in this country.
I think the minister, even though he does not think that the Times should have any interest in this matter, may agree that their comments are not without a certain amount of common sense. I will read on, because again I think the points are so well made that they cannot be improved on:
The American attitude in these negotiations has reflected the difficulties of the American government over the renewal of the reciprocal trade act and the bill for the simplification of the tariff. Rather than accept the amendments by the house of representatives to the reciprocal trade act the president may use his veto.
Later on this comment touches on the difference in the relation between preference and tariff, and puts it in what I thought was a rather pointed way. It says:
In view of the present uncertainties this country must weigh with the utmost care the obligations which are imposed upon it by the general agreement. This is especially necessary now because the next meeting of the members in the autumn may be concerned with trying to give permanent form to the present temporary organization.
If a permanent organization is to be set up, this country cannot allow the status of preferences to be left, as it is at present, inferior to the status of tariffs. The illogicality of the American attitude to imperial preference is illustrated by the American support of the Schuman plan,-
Hon. members will recall that the Schuman plan is that much discussed plan proposed by Schuman of the French government in an attempt to integrate particularly French and German, and also other minor European countries', iron and steel industries. Last summer it looked as though it was likely to break down because of lack of sympathy from Britain; but by reason of recent changes which they have made, it now seems likely to succeed. I continue:
The illogicality of the American attitude to imperial preference is illustrated by the American support of the Schuman plan, which sets out to create a new free trade area in Europe and is at least as likely to hinder as to help the more general extension of freer trade. Certainly, Europe cannot be regarded as a more satisfactory economic unit than the commonwealth; the countries of the commonwealth, in fact, are naturally still more complementary than are the predominantly industrial countries of western Europe.
There is one further quote I wish to make because it is on the same point. It says this, speaking again of the American attitude towards the Schuman plan:
The cause of freer trade can only be hampered by illogical and one-sided distinctions of this sort;

and if the Schuman plan is a portent and the future lies not with many-sided free trade but with regional pacts, then the preservation of the bonds within the commonwealth will become even more vital for this country than it already is.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have read these extracts because it seems to me that the points which they raise are very practical, and they are particularly underlined by reason of what the leader of the opposition said this afternoon regarding the meeting of Canadian businessmen and their desire to have a conference on commonwealth trade. The setting up of this free trade area in Europe, if that is what it comes to be, may actually hinder rather than help the task of freeing world trade.
Of course, there is another thing which comes into this, and which I should like to refer to briefly, namely, the everlasting question of bulk trade agreements. That of course is one of the things that bother them in Britain, and it is one of the things that bother us here. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, if you can still refer to him in that way, said very frankly when w'e were talking about the wheat agreement-I think it was the wheat agreement we were discussing in this house some weeks ago-"If we had known four or five years ago as much as we know now we might not have done quite the same thing." According to farmers' present seeding intentions it is down by-
That is the wheat acreage. I continue:

But in the main the explanation is simply this: The other crops are offering the farmer the chance of making more money. Their price has improved, responding as it does to the influences that make themselves felt in a free market. As compared with this time two years ago, the price of oats is now 14 cents higher; barley is four cents higher; rye is 87 cents higher and flax is 82 cents higher. Mr. Speaker, I believe in freer trade-I always have, and I hope I always shall. So far as this Torquay agreement goes-well, certainly I do not think any member in the house could find very much objection to it. Whatever steps they have taken must be accepted as progress, although we may be disappointed in the degree of that progress. I think, indeed, that everyone has been disappointed.
This would include even the chairman of the Canadian delegation, Mr. Wilgress, who, according to a Reuters dispatch, said on April 21 that the results were not as great as many had hoped, and pointed out that governments had been hesitant about agreeing to substantial reductions in duties.
As I understand, the chief disappointment in the agreement is that Great Britain and the United States could not get together in a sort of tariff-lowering pact. Had they been able to do that, other countries automatically would have benefited. We had all hoped there would be a kind of softening of the lines of division between the sterling and dollar areas. Instead however I think it is correct to say that those lines have been hardened; and every hon. member knows the implications that has for Canada.

I say that despite the concessions which we have obtained from the United States at these three conferences the American tariff level is still considerably higher than the Canadian. The effect of Torquay, Geneva and Annecy is that it will facilitate the entry of more United States goods into Canada without bringing the United States tariff to a point where Canadian manufacturers can compete in the United States market. I think Canadians are going to be disappointed that something has not been said about armaments. I understood that Canada was going to manufacture arms for the United States. Now it appears that all we are going to make now is parts. I do not know if there is a tariff on munitions that we export to the United States. I assume there is. Perhaps this is one item on which we should have received a concession in these critical times.	.
I say again that the Canadian government vas bested at Torquay by our United States friends, if you judge by the dollar value of the concessions obtained. I think at this time it is proper that we should consider the state of our trade with the United States. I would not deny for a moment the tremendous strides which the government has made in building up our exports to the United States. The fact that they have been able to build up our exports in that market, the most competitive in the world, is no mean achievement, and I do not wish to detract from it. Nevertheless when we recall that in 1950 two-thirds of our exports went to the United States we can see the dangers inherent in the situation. This afternoon the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said we were something like the man who put all his eggs in one basket. That is what we have done so far as our trade is concerned today. As has been pointed out already, the United States market has never been known as the most stable market in the world. Actually the opposite is true. It is subject to economic recessions, and going by past history, tariff policy can change overnight. I wonder what would happen to Canada if suddenly General MacArthur or Mr. Taft should become president of the United States. I think then we might have to worry immediately about higher American tariffs. Therefore I say one of our objectives in tariff and trade policy should be to diversify our trade to a greater extent in future.
The minister or some of his friends may ask how we can do that. Well, there are many possibilities. I have in my hand a

clipping from the Financial Post of April 14, which states that France offers to exchange steel for our newsprint. They want our newsprint, most of which is going to the United States. We are pretty short of steel. There may be objections to such a procedure; perhaps the price of French steel is too high, or there may be other reasons why that is not feasible, but on the surface this would seem to be one way by which we might diversify our trade.
Our second chief trade problem today is the British market. A great deal has been said already about the deteriorating position of that market. In 1949 United Kingdom sales to Canada were only 43 per cent of her purchases from this country. In 1950 they were 85 per cent. Before the war Britain used to take nearly half our exports. Last year she took only one-third, and I think it is safe to say that all hon. members are alarmed at the way our exports to Britain have deteriorated. Prior to the war the British bought a great deal from us. Since the war they have not been able to buy as much simply because they lacked the Canadian dollars with which to make those purchases. British statesmen and opposition leaders in this house have warned the Canadian government repeatedly as to what would happen if we did not permit them to earn more Canadian dollars. To give only one illustration, I remember a Canadian Press dispatch back in 1949, which said:
Cripps issues warning Canada to lose exports unless it "buys British."
Britain will buy less food from Canada unless Canada buys more from Britain, Sir Stafford Cripps, chancellor of the exchequer, said Thursday.
. . . he said the crux of the post-war Anglo-Canadian trading problems is expansion of British exports to Canada.
At that time, two years ago, Sir Stafford Cripps put the trade problem as far as England was concerned right up to this parliament. If Canada wanted to hold the British market he told us we had to buy from them. However in the intervening years, our government has been most apathetic in trying to increase British imports. As a matter of fact this government has taken several steps which have had the opposite effect. For instance, several years ago our government encouraged the British to send textiles to Canada. They said that in order to encourage that trade they would remove the tariff. The British textile industry went to work and produced at competitive prices, and began to earn a great many Canadian dollars. As soon as they began to do that our government decided to put the tariff back on again. Much the same thing happened in the

automobile industry. Ever since the end of the war one cabinet minister after another, one government spokesman after another, has been urging British industry to become competitive, to get their prices down; yet when the British automobile industry did begin to compete, when they did produce a car that could be sold in the Canadian market, right away our government put on a dumping duty.
I cannot reconcile actions like those with a desire to increase British imports, and increase trade within the commonwealth. I think it is fitting also to mention what happened as far as our wheat agreement was concerned. The British government made an agreement in writing with the Canadian government to buy wheat at a fixed price. They fulfilled the terms of their agreement, and did so in writing; yet numerous members of this house accused the British of reneging, of failing to live up to a moral obligation, I do not suppose the British liked such statements very much. I think we in this house should remember that our chief market for farm products in the past has been Britain, as it probably will be in the future. When we do things like that and make statements like those in this house, I suggest that we are jeopardizing that market. Insulting your customers is not a good way to build up trade. I do not think you could do it in any other kind of business.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear now that another world-wide, multilateral trade conference like Torquay is most unlikely. If that is the case, any additional concessions we get must come from direct negotiations. Therefore I agree with other hon. members who have suggested that we should commence further trade negotiations with Britain. Probably we should do the same thing with the United States, and possibly with France and: other countries. Our first objective in these negotiations should be to get back our old, traditional markets, and our second objective, the diversification of our trade. If we can do these things, our trade in future will remain in a healthy position.

Mr. Speaker, tonight I am not going to presume to assess the results which may or may not have been achieved in the Torquay agreements. We have had many discussions of these trade agreements in the past, as was pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), running from Geneva to Annecy and now to Torquay, and we are led to hope that much good will come out of this one. That is something that can be perhaps better determined by the committee to which this matter will be
Trade Agreements
referred; and certainly we in the house will be in a better position to discuss the question after that committee has performed the functions required of it. However, I do suggest there are one or two questions raised by this report, some of them perhaps of particular interest to the east, to which I should refer tonight.
In connection with these agreements we see that some special arrangements are made with respect to Cuba. We are told that we will purchase some 75,000 tons of sugar annually for the next three years, and it is hoped that as a result we will be able to at least partially regain the position we held at one time in the Cuban market, but which unfortunately we lost. Just what we are going to gain by the concessions given us by Cuba is not clear; that is one of the questions the committee will have to determine. At one time that was a very satisfactory market for our potatoes, and it also took large quantities of fish products from eastern Canada. Then in the late twenties the government of this country negotiated a treaty with the British West Indies, no doubt thinking it was accomplishing a great deal in the development of our trade. I think most Canadians, however, and particularly those in the east will have to admit that as a result of that British West Indies treaty we gained very few benefits, and certainly we lost our markets in Cuba. If by these negotiations at Torquay the government has taken steps to rectify that position it certainly will be an advantage to us.
Then another question is raised. The British West Indies treaty has been in effect since 1927 or 1928. We built a fleet of ships, which we have subsidized. We have spent a great deal of money attempting to develop trade between Canada and the West Indies; but now we see that Mr. Donald Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways, says that tremendous decisions will have to be made this year. He hopes parliament will provide money to cover the deficit of last year, which I believe was something like $845,000, but he doubts whether further deficits of this size can be covered in this way. More than that, he points out the fact that replacement of ships now in the British West Indian-Canadian service will have to be made if the treaty is to be maintained. Now, sir, there is a serious question.
The second question arising out of this one dealing with Cuba is: having once more sought to regain the Cuban market, are we also going to maintain the developments which we have achieved in the West Indian market? Certainly, there have been some definite advantages gained, particularly to

Trade Agreements
eastern Canada. One of the questions to which I am sure this house, or at any rate the government, will have to determine before many weeks go by is what will be our position with respect to the British West Indian trade in the future. Are we prepared to make the capital expenditure which will ultimately be necessary if these advantages are to be maintained?
There is one ray of sunshine that some of us may see in Torquay, perhaps a minor one. Those in the east, at least in my constituency, will note with some satisfaction that apparently trade arrangements have been made with western Germany. At one time the German market was of tremendous importance to us in the valley in so far as the shipment of apples was concerned. During the years immediately preceding the last war we shipped large quantities of apples there. Of course, that market has been lost to us. We would be interested, and I know the house will be interested, in determining just what advantages we derive under Torquay from the apparent beginnings which we are making towards the resumption of trade with western Germany. But generally, Mr. Speaker, I think that Torquay leaves one with a great deal of disappointment.
This afternoon the member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred to the triangle from Canada to Great Britain to the United States and back, which has developed over a period of many years. It has been of tremendous importance to all of Canada, but particularly to eastern Canada. Sometimes when we talk politically of the imperial preference one gathers the inference that imperial preference was something which developed under the aegis of the late Viscount Bennett. Our friends are sometimes disposed to shrug their shoulders, as if it were something of which they were not too proud. Of course, we know that imperial preference has been written into our tariff laws through generations. The preference was established by a Liberal government back in the days of Mr. Paterson, who was minister of finance. When Mr. Fielding was minister of finance we had the first imperial preference budget. It was written, into our trade throughout the years, but we received no corresponding benefit from Britain, because she was a free trade country. Throughout the years, we did everything to develop that trade, and1 we succeeded in so doing.
Then in the thirties the matter developed still further, but today we have to face the fact, as suggested by the member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) a moment ago, that after Torquay it looks as if these conferences have reached the limit of their resources. From reports we have had about Torquay the
[Mr. Nowlan.l
United States, quite properly, was insisting on the one hand that imperial preference be reduced or be abolished, while on the other hand you had certain commonwealth countries such as the United Kingdom, New Zealand and South Africa refusing to compromise or to do anything with respect to these imperial preferences.

speechtext: Good for them.

speechtext:
We in this country, because of our geographical position-I am not criticizing for the moment but I think this is a fact-felt we had to make some compromise between the two positions, and we did give away, rightly or wrongly, the preference on some two hundred articles or more in order to get some hoped for benefits out of the United States market. Whatever the situation may be, sir, we know that trade on the triangle has virtually gone. Figures have been given, and I do not want to weary the house with respect to them again, but our trade with Great Britain has diminished until last year our exports to Great Britain fell off some thirty-four per cent; our exports to other countries, outside of the United States, fell off by some twenty per cent, whereas our exports to the United States increased to a substantial degree. Instead of a triangle you have at the best a two-way street. For the sake of argument I will admit for the moment it is a two-way street, but it is a street, sir, which could be mined very easily. It is a street on which land blocks could be established, if not an iron curtain dropped. We could very easily find ourselves in the position where it became a one-way street or no street at all but simply a meandering path on which the grass will grow. Then, our trade will wither and disappear, because we have lost those traditional markets to which we have been accustomed; markets which we in the east have to depend upon if our economy is going to be maintained. It is for that reason we look upon Torquay with misgiving and with doubt.
So far as these concessions are concerned we feel that our government has gone about as far as it felt it could go. Other conference countries, commonwealth countries, refused to go that far. The United States has refused to go any farther. We know that sooner or later this government, or some other government, will have to make up its mind just what position we are going to take in the trading of the world in the future. Certainly, we hope for multilateral trade. Certainly, we hope for a lessening of the trade barriers. But, sir, I think we have to be practical. Living in this world today we have to realize how, not fantastic perhaps, but how very flimsy may be these hopes. This preference is more than a matter of trade to those of us

in the east. Written into the trade agreements of the past there is the benefit of direct shipment, and the fact that preference will only apply to shipments made from the ports of origin in the commonwealth to a port on a river, lake or seaboard in Canada without transshipment.
In his statement the other night the Minister of Finance stated we had safeguarded the principle of preference. I am not quarrelling with that for the moment at all. It is for the future to determine. Since we gave away the benefits on at least two hundred items, then we automatically lost the benefits of direct shipment on those articles coming into Canada. They will now go into New York or Boston.

I am not asserting we are.
I am asserting that if we are, then that follows. This committee can determine that after the matter has been referred to it. I can tell the right hon. gentleman that papers which have not been entirely critical of this government have certainly suggested that is one of the outcomes of any relaxation of the imperial preference which follows because of Torquay. But we are not debating what may or may not happen. At the moment we are debating the realities of the situation, and the fact that we in Canada are facing an extremely serious trade situation because of the emphasis upon our United States trade and the diminution of our trade with the United Kingdom, the commonwealth countries and other countries outside of the continent of North America.
This afternoon the leader of the opposition referred to the statement issued: out of Toronto last Saturday by the British-Canadian trade group which has been studying our problems, and which had recommended and urged the establishment or the creation of a conference between the governments of the commonwealth in order to study this problem and to attempt to resolve it. Certainly I suggest that we all should support that proposal. If there ever was a time when such a conference was necessary, it is now. No stone should be left unturned. I realize that there are difficulties in the way. I realize that it is not an easy problem to solve. But the more difficult the problem, the more reason for prompt action and the less reason for delay. Having regard to the seriousness of the situation, and in view of the discussions which have taken place here today, I would hope that this government would take some steps to support the suggestion and to urge and to lead in the establishment of such a study in the immediate future.
Ancillary to that, may I say that I was intrigued to read in a press report the statement by the president, I think it was, of the British federation of agriculture-because agriculture, industry and trade were all represented at Toronto. The head of the British agricultural group suggested that the time had come when there should be, and would be on the part of the British government, greater relaxation of trade restrictions in so far as the importation of Canadian food products are concerned. I know the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) must have studied that statement with some particular interest.
In that statement some reference was made to the fact that the cheese contract showed

Trade Agreements
a relaxation at least on the part of the British of their fixed determination to engage in bulk purchases. Those of us in the apple industry know that last year Great Britain relaxed the restrictions upon the importation of apples from all the sterling areas. In other words, New Zealand, South Africa and Australia exported their apples to the trade in Great Britain, and the apples were .bought and sold direct without restriction; possibly that was only because they were in the sterling areas. But it has been suggested by more than one competent authority, or at least has been suggested, by one who had information on the matter, on Friday night in Toronto, that this coming year arrangements could be made whereby Great Britain would import apples from Canada, independent of and apart from bulk purchases and for distribution direct to the trade.
The minister will know that last year importations were made and that purchases of apples were made direct from the trade in British Columbia and Nova Scotia, without the intervention of this government; and that was a step in the right direction. I suggest that there is now more than a possibility and that apparently, according to these men who are now here, there is a probability that, if we take the right steps and follow the right course, this year we can arrange for the direct sale of apples from Canada- from British Columbia and from Nova Scotia; those are the two great exporting, production areas-to Great Britain, to the trade there. It has been suggested that a mission ought to be set up there, representative of the two apple exporting areas, to handle our apples and to sell them direct to the trade. If that could be done, it would be of tremendous importance to the apple producers not only of British Columbia, I assume, but certainly of Nova Scotia.
We know that there are governmental committees engaged on various projects. We know that there is always consideration given to the problem of the dollar and sterling areas. We know that each year during the past two years the British-after discussion, after debate, after waiting, after the apples were probably picked, when no one knew whether they were going to be, sold or not-made an agreement whereby they purchased a substantial quantity of our apples. I suggest that this year we take time by the forelock, that we do not wait until the frosts come next fall, that we pursue the matter now and that, if possible, we make arrangements so that the apples may be sold, in order that the producers will know of it well in advance.

Those are some of the minor and perhaps ancillary matters arising out of the discussion this afternoon of the Torquay agreement. By dealing with these matters, and by working at them unitedly and intelligently, we can and must solve the problem of regaining these markets in the sterling area; otherwise the economy of eastern Canada at least will be most seriously impaired in the future.
